title: MAIN PAL versus STATE OF HARYANA
case_title: Main Pal v. State of Haryana
neutral_facts: The accused was charged with trespassing into the house of a woman and assaulting her with intent to outrage her modesty. The evidence, however, indicated that the accused had assaulted the woman's daughter-in-law to outrage her modesty. The accused defended himself against the charge of assaulting the woman and focused his cross-examination on proving that he did not assault or outrage the modesty of the woman. The prosecution's case was that the accused had touched and caught the hand of the daughter-in-law and fled when she raised an alarm. The Court concluded that the accused was prejudiced by the error in the charge and directed a new trial after framing a charge against the daughter-in-law.
offence_severity: Minimum: 6 months rigorous imprisonment, Maximum: 1 year rigorous imprisonment
physical_harm: No injuries or death caused
number_of_offences: 2 offences charged, 2 offences upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence indicated that the accused assaulted PW1's daughter-in-law to outrage her modesty, and the court accepted that the accused was not charged with an offence against her but was tried for it, leading to a failure of justice.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of PW1 and PW2, noting that their evidence showed the accused did not touch or abuse PW1, but touched PW1's daughter-in-law, leading to the conclusion that the accused was misled by the charge.
trial_duration: The accused was tried from 23.3.1996, the trial judgment was dated 2.2.2001, the High Court decision was on 16.3.2010, and the Supreme Court decision was on 7.9.2010.
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Vikas Sharma, K.M. Gupta, Praveen Swarup; Counsel for the State: Not stated.
investigation_status: FIR registered on 23.3.1996, charge sheet filed, trial completed.
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Convicted under Sections 452 and 354 IPC, sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and a fine of Rs.1,000/-', 'high_court': 'Upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence from six to four months rigorous imprisonment', 'supreme_court': 'Allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction, and remitted the matter for a new trial'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused could be punished for assaulting and outraging the modesty of PW1's daughter-in-law, even though he was not charged with any offence with reference to PW1's daughter-in-law, on the ground that the error or omission in the charge did not prejudice the accused or result in failure of justice.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the accused was not required to defend himself against a charge that he assaulted and outraged the modesty of PW1's daughter-in-law, as the charge levelled against him was not proved, and thus he ought to have been acquitted.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the principles of fair play and natural justice embodied in Sections 211, 212, 215 and 464 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, emphasizing that an accused should know what is the charge against him to build his defence and that the main concern is whether the accused had a fair trial.
precedent_relied_upon: Willie (William) Staney v. State of Madhya Pradesh AIR 1956 SC 116; Gurbachan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1957 SC 623; Shamnsaheb M. Multtani vs. State of Karnataka 2001 (2) SCC 577; State of West Bengal vs. Laisal Haque AIR 1989 SC 129; State of A.P. vs. Thakkidiram Reddy 1998 (6) SCC 554; Dalbir Singh v. State of UP 2004 (5) SCC 334; Dumpala Chandra Reddy vs. Nimakayala Bali Reddy 2008 (8) SCC 339 and Sanichar Sahni vs. State of Bihar 2009 (7) sec 198
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
other_sentence_order: The matter is remitted to the trial court with a direction for a new trial after framing a charge by substituting the words 'her daughter-in-law Sheela Devi' for the words 'abovenamed Prakashi Devi', in the second part of the charge.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused was charged with trespassing into the house of a woman and assaulting her with intent to outrage her modesty. The evidence, however, indicated that the accused had assaulted the woman's daughter-in-law to outrage her modesty. The accused defended himself against the charge of assaulting the woman and focused his cross-examination on proving that he did not assault or outrage the modesty of the woman. The prosecution's case was that the accused had touched and caught the hand of the daughter-in-law and fled when she raised an alarm. The trial court convicted the accused under sections 452 and 354 of the IPC, but the High Court upheld the conviction. The Supreme Court, however, held that the charge was incorrect as it did not mention the daughter-in-law, and the accused was not aware of the charge against her. The Court concluded that the accused was prejudiced by the error in the charge and directed a new trial after framing a charge against the daughter-in-law.

title: SATYA NARAYANA TIWARI AND ANR. versus STATE OF U.P.
case_title: Satya Narayana Tiwari And Anr. v. State of U.P.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B, s.498-A; Dowry Prohibition Act s.4
aggravating_circumstances: Demand for dowry, persistent harassment, cruelty, burning and strangulation
neutral_facts: The accused, a husband and his mother-in-law, were charged with the death of a bride who died of strangulation and burn injuries in her matrimonial home. The deceased, aged about 24 years, died within three years of her marriage. The father of the deceased stated in the FIR that dowry was being demanded, specifically a Maruti car. The deceased was subjected to harassment and maltreatment by the accused due to the demand for dowry, which persisted after about six months of marriage. The deceased was found in her bedroom with signs of violence, including ligature marks and burn injuries. The accused were found to have committed the crime, with the mother-in-law falsely reporting the death as a suicide. The prosecution established that the accused caused the death through strangulation and burning, which was a case of dowry death.
offence_severity: 3 years rigorous imprisonment under Section 498A, and six months rigorous imprisonment under Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. Life sentence under Section 304-B IPC
physical_harm: Strangulation and burn injuries
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged and finally upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning as the accused committed the crime with preplanning and lodged a false report to misguide the machinery of law
motive: Demand of dowry in the form of a Maruti Car
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the circumstantial evidence that the deceased was subjected to cruelty and harassment by her husband and mother-in-law for the demand of a Maruti Car, which persisted and led to her death by strangulation and burning.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the testimony of PW 1 and PW 2 (the father and son-in-law of the deceased) as credible regarding the illegal demand of a Maruti Car and the subsequent harassment and maltreatment of the deceased.
post_offence_conduct: The accused absconded after the incident and only surrendered to court several days later, which the court considered as abnormal conduct for innocent persons.
trial_duration: FIR lodged on 03.11.2000, trial court acquitted accused, High Court convicted on 12.07.2005, Supreme Court judgment on 28.10.2010
legal_representation: Indu Malhotra, Rajesh and Vivek Jain for the Appellants; K.T.S. Tulsi, Shail Kr. Dwivedi, AAG, R.K. Gupta, Pradeep Misra, Suraj Singh, Vandana Mishra, Anurag Dubey, Meenesh Dube, Ravinder Singh and S.R. Setia for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR lodged, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Conviction; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal, upheld High Court's conviction
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased's death was caused by strangulation and burn injuries within seven years of her marriage, and that she was subjected to cruelty and harassment by her husband and mother-in-law for the demand of dowry. The persistent demand for a Maruti car and the subsequent harassment and torture by the accused were established through credible testimony. The prosecution also highlighted the presence of circumstantial evidence, including the half-burnt cloth with a knot around the neck and the burnt cordless phone, which ruled out the theory of suicide.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the deceased's death was a case of suicide, citing the presence of a half-burnt cloth with a knot around the neck and the absence of direct evidence linking the accused to the crime. They also claimed that the trial court's acquittal was based on a superfluous approach and that the knot around the deceased's neck was not produced before the court, which they argued was a ground against the prosecution.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle from Kunhiabdulla v. State of Kerala, which outlined the essential ingredients for the application of Section 304-B IPC, including the death of a woman caused by burns or bodily injury, occurring within seven years of marriage, and the cruelty or harassment by the husband or his relatives in connection with dowry demands, which must have occurred soon before her death.
precedent_relied_upon: Kunhiabdulla v. State of Kerala, 2004 (4) SCC 13
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the case was considered a rarest of rare case of bride burning, which is brutal and barbaric. Although the prosecution did not level a charge under Section 302 IPC, the court deemed such cases deserving of death sentence due to their severity.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The court considered the brutal and barbaric nature of the crime, the persistent demand for dowry, the cruelty and harassment inflicted on the deceased, and the fact that the crime was premeditated and involved multiple perpetrators.
other_sentence_order: The court cancelled the bail bonds of the accused and ordered them to be taken into custody to serve the remaining period of their sentence. The court also allowed the application for impleadment.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a husband and his mother-in-law, were charged with the death of a bride who died of strangulation and burn injuries in her matrimonial home. The deceased, aged about 24 years, died within three years of her marriage. The father of the deceased stated in the FIR that dowry was being demanded, specifically a Maruti car. The trial court acquitted the accused, but the High Court convicted them under sections 304-B and 498-A of the IPC and section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. The deceased was subjected to harassment and maltreatment by the accused due to the demand for dowry, which persisted after about six months of marriage. The accused were found to have committed the crime, with the mother-in-law falsely reporting the death as a suicide. The prosecution established that the accused caused the death through strangulation and burning, which was a case of dowry death.

title: UTTAM CHAKRABORTY versus STATE OF ASSAM
case_title: Uttam Chakraborty v. State of Assam
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of murder, death sentence for one accused, life imprisonment for the other
neutral_facts: The accused-husband and his friend were friends. The accused-husband was married to a woman who was pregnant. The couple had a child who was about 4 or 5 years old. The deceased was employed as a school teacher and had engaged a domestic help who resided in their house. The prosecution alleged that the accused-husband and the domestic help had an illicit relationship, which led to frequent quarrels between the couple. On the night of the incident, the domestic help's mother was informed that her daughter had fallen ill and accompanied them to the police station. There, she learned that her daughter had died of burn injuries and lodged a FIR. During the investigation, it was found that the accused-husband was present when the deceased died. The prosecution relied primarily on the testimony of the child witness and the domestic help, as well as the post-mortem report indicating severe injuries and the removal of the foetus.

title: STATE OF A. P. versus M. SOHAN BABU & ANR.

title: MUNNAWAR AND ORS. versus STATE OF U.P. ETC.
case_title: Munnawar and Ors. v. State of U.P. Etc.
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of Section 302, convicted under Section 307
neutral_facts: The accused fired a shot at the victim during an incident that occurred while the victim and his brother were on their way to a court hearing. The victim was seriously injured and taken to a hospital, where he was examined by a doctor. A dying declaration was recorded by an executive magistrate, which detailed the identity of the assailants, the weapon used, and the site of the injury. The victim succumbed to his injuries after five days, with the cause of death attributed to septicemia resulting from the gunshot wound. The prosecution relied on the testimony of the victim's brother and other witnesses, as well as the dying declaration and medical evidence.
offence_severity: Minimum 10 years, Maximum Life Imprisonment or Death
physical_harm: Death of victim due to septicemia caused by gunshot injuries
number_of_offences: Three counts charged, two upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The dying declaration recorded by the Executive Magistrate gave full details as to the identity of the assailants, the weapons used, the site of the injury and the fact that he was brought to the hospital by a neighbour and his elder brother who were accompanying him at the time of incident. The doctor who was looking after the deceased when the dying declaration was recorded gave a certificate that he was fully conscious and lucid at the time of its recording.
witness_credibility: The promptness in recording of FIR would belie the doubt as to the presence of eyewitness-informant at the place of incident. The presence of the two eye witnesses is accepted as they were accompanying the deceased to court and the promptness of the FIR reflects their presence.
trial_duration: The incident took place on 20th May 2000. The FIR was lodged on 20th May 2000 at 12 noon. The trial court judgment was on 8th August 2007. The High Court decision was on 8th August 2007. The Supreme Court judgment was on 5th May 2010.
legal_representation: Sushil Kumar, Manoj Prasad, Aditya Kumar for the Appellants. T.N. Singh, Rajiv Dubey, Kamlendra Mishra for the Respondent.
investigation_status: FIR lodged on 20th May 2000 at 12 noon. Charge-sheet filed. Trial completed.
appeal_history: Trial court acquitted the appellants of offence under Section 302 IPC but convicted them under Section 307 IPC. High Court convicted appellants for offence under Section 302/149 IPC. Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased, along with PW-1 and PW-2, was on the way to court to attend a case. The appellants armed with a pistol fired a shot at the deceased and then ran away. The deceased was seriously injured and taken to the hospital. The FIR was lodged promptly, and the presence of eyewitnesses was confirmed. The injuries were grievous and sufficient to cause death, and the dying declaration was reliable.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the first dying declaration recorded by the police officer did not have the endorsement of a doctor and was therefore unreliable. They also claimed that the second dying declaration was not properly endorsed and that the medical evidence showed the death was due to septicemia caused by the injuries, not the initial gunshot wound. They further argued that the eye witnesses were not present at the scene and that the case should be under Section 307 IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration recorded by a Magistrate duly endorsed by a Doctor should not be discarded unless there are suspicious circumstances. The Court emphasized that the reliability of the dying declaration depends on the facts of the case and the evidence produced.
precedent_relied_upon: Balak Ram v. State of U.P. 1975(3) SCC 219; K. Ramachandra Reddy & Anr. v. The Public Prosecutor 1976(3) SCC 618
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the injuries were grievous and sufficient to cause death, and the dying declaration was reliable. The Court found that the trial court had erred in concluding that the doctor's negligence caused the death, and the High Court's conviction under Section 302/149 IPC was upheld.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused fired a shot at the victim during an incident that occurred while the victim and his brother were on their way to a court hearing. The victim was seriously injured and taken to a hospital, where he was examined by a doctor. A dying declaration was recorded by an executive magistrate, which detailed the identity of the assailants, the weapon used, and the site of the injury. The victim succumbed to his injuries after five days, with the cause of death attributed to septicemia resulting from the gunshot wound. The prosecution relied on the testimony of the victim's brother and other witnesses, as well as the dying declaration and medical evidence. The trial court acquitted the accused of murder but convicted them under Section 307 for causing grievous harm. The High Court overturned this decision and convicted the accused under Section 302/149 for murder.

title: NORTHERN MINERAL LTD. versus UNION OF INDIA AND ANR.
case_title: NORTHERN MINERAL LTD. v. UNION OF INDIA AND ANR.
statutory_provisions: Insecticides Act, 1968 ss.24(3) and 24(4); Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 s.245
neutral_facts: The accused, a company manufacturing insecticides, was served with a report from a regional laboratory stating that a sample of their insecticide did not conform to specifications. The accused notified their intention to adduce evidence in controversion of the report. However, the sample was not sent for re-analysis by the central laboratory due to the insecticide's shelf life expiring before the complaint was filed. The accused argued that the shelf life expiration rendered further testing futile, and that the prosecution was an abuse of the court process.

number_of_offences: Not stated

witness_credibility: The court assessed that the accused had notified its intention to adduce evidence in controversion of the report, which took the report out of the class of 'conclusive evidence' and conferred the right to have the sample tested by the Central Insecticides Laboratory.

title: SIKANDAR SINGH & ORS. versus STATE OF BIHAR
case_title: Sikandar Singh & Ors. v. State of Bihar
aggravating_circumstances: Common object of unlawful assembly, use of lethal weapons
neutral_facts: The accused were part of an unlawful assembly with a common object to eliminate the deceased and his brother. offence_severity: Minimum: Death (Section 302 IPC), Maximum: Life imprisonment (Section 302 IPC) and 10 years (Section 307 IPC)
physical_harm: One victim died at the spot; another received injuries but survived

key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the testimony of PW-4 and PW-5, and the nature of the weapons possessed by the accused, which indicated they formed an unlawful assembly with a common object of eliminating the deceased and his brother.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, particularly PW-4 and PW-5, whose testimony was relied upon to establish the case against the accused.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was passed on 07.06.2001 and 12.06.2001 by the Additional Sessions Judge, Bhojpur. The High Court of Judicature at Patna delivered its judgment and order on 03.09.2004. The Supreme Court decision was dated 09.07.2010.

title: SHAM @ KISHOR BHASKARRAO MATKARI versus THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
case_title: Sham@ Kishor Bhaskarrao Matkari v. State of Maharashtra
aggravating_circumstances: Victims were defenceless, assault on children, premeditated attack, false story by accused, no third person involved, brutal nature of injuries, accused slept with victims
mitigating_circumstances: No pre-plan or premeditation, unblemished antecedents, no weapon used, not a rarest of rare case
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 and s.307 IPC, sentenced to life imprisonment and 7 years
high_court_outcome: Confirmed conviction, enhanced sentence to death
neutral_facts: The accused and his brother resided together in a rented house. A dispute over property led to a quarrel between the accused and his brother. The accused, after a confrontation, returned to the house during the night and assaulted his brother, his brother's wife, and their children. The victims were found dead or injured in the house, with signs of burns and head injuries. The accused was found with bloodstains on his hands and clothes. The police arrived and took the accused to the hospital. The accused made a statement to the Executive Magistrate admitting to the killings. Medical experts confirmed the cause of death and injuries.
physical_harm: Three murders and injuries to two children, including partial burns to the wife
number_of_offences: Five counts charged, three upheld (murders) and two (attempted murders) upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found no pre-plan or premeditation, the quarrel started due to a land dispute
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence and other material on record clearly establish the guilt of the accused, including the statement of the accused before the Executive Magistrate, the version of PW-7 who witnessed the occurrence, neighbors and the landlord (PWs 1 and 3), and the opinion of the doctors (PWs-6 and 11) along with the recovery of a stone inside the house of 'MK'.
witness_credibility: There is no reason to disbelieve the version of PW-7 who witnessed the occurrence, neighbors and the landlord (PWs 1 and 3) as well as the confessional statement of the accused before the Executive Magistrate.
custody_duration: He is in jail since 30.06.2001 and in the death cell since the date of the judgment of the High Court, that is, 03.05.2006.
trial_duration: The trial court convicted the accused u/ss 302 and 307 IPC and sentenced him to imprisonment for life and 7 years under the two counts respectively. legal_representation: Tara Chand Sharma, Mahabir Singh Mangla, Uma Datta, H Kishan Datta and Neelam Sharma for the Appellant. Sushi! Karanjkar, Sachin Patil, Sanjay Kharde,. Sankar A Chillarge, Asha Gopalan Nair for the Respondent.
investigation_status: Charge-sheet was laid in the Court of Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Bhusawal, who committed the case to the Court of Sessions.
appeal_history: The trial court convicted the accused u/ss 302 and 307 IPC and sentenced him to imprisonment for life and 7 years under the two counts respectively. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the accused and allowed that of the State for enhancement of sentence and while confirming the conviction, awarded the death sentence to the accused. The Supreme Court set aside the death penalty imposed by the High Court and restored the life imprisonment awarded by the trial court.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused caused the death of his brother, sister-in-law, and nephew, and attempted to murder two other children. The evidence and other material on record clearly establish the guilt of the accused, and the prosecution has established its case beyond reasonable doubt for an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the accused had no pre-plan or pre-meditation to eliminate the family of his brother. The quarrel started due to a land dispute, and the accused was sleeping with the other victims in the same house on the fateful night. The accused has unblemished antecedents, and the case is not a rarest of rare case.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the death penalty should be imposed only in the rarest of rare cases, considering both aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh vs. State of Punjab, (1980) 2 SCC 684; Machhi Singh and Others vs. State of Punjab, (1983) 3 SCC 470; C. Muniappan and Others vs. State of Tamil Nadu, 2010 (10) SCR 262 = (2010) 9 SCC 567; Ajitsingh Hamamsingh Gujral vs. State of Maharashtra, JT 2011 (10) SC 465
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court's enhancement of the sentence to death was not supported by adequate and acceptable reasons. The trial court's life imprisonment was deemed appropriate, and the case was not a rarest of rare case.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The accused had no pre-plan or pre-meditation to eliminate the family of his brother, had unblemished antecedents, and was jobless at the time of the incident. The accused was in jail for over 10 years and could be reformed or rehabilitated.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The accused caused the death of three persons, assaulted the victims at midnight when they were asleep, and showed extreme brutality. The accused remained silent in the house despite the victims being killed and children injured, and did not raise alarm.

The trial court convicted the accused for murder and attempted murder, sentencing him to life imprisonment and seven years. The High Court upheld the conviction but enhanced the sentence to death.

title: RAKESH & ANOTHER versus STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
case_title: RAKESH & ANR. v. STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Section 302 IPC, sentenced to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The prosecution case was that two appellants, along with another accused, caused the death of the victim by assaulting him with sharp edged weapons. The victim was taken to the hospital where he was examined by a doctor and declared dead. The accused were arrested, and the weapons used in the crime were recovered on their disclosure statements. The Court also noted that the witness's testimony was trustworthy and that the prosecution case was supported by other evidence, including the statements of the Investigating Officer and the recovery of weapons.
physical_harm: Death caused by sharp edged weapons
number_of_offences: Three offences charged, three upheld
motive: Appellant no.1 wanted utensils from the deceased
key_evidence_accepted: The court accepted the testimony of PW.11, the nephew of the deceased, as a natural witness whose account of the incident was detailed and consistent with other evidence such as the statements of the Investigating Officer (PW.21) and PW.9, the arrest of the accused, and recovery of weapons on their disclosure statements.
witness_credibility: PW.11 was assessed as a trustworthy and natural witness despite being closely related to the deceased. His testimony was found to be reliable even after grilling cross-examination and despite minor discrepancies in witness accounts.
trial_duration: Offence: 5.3.1996; Trial judgment: 21.2.1997; High Court decision: 10.2.2005; Supreme Court decision: 15.12.2006
legal_representation: Siddharth Aggarwal, Aditya Wadhoa, Stui Gujral, Senthil Jagadeesan for the Appellant; Vibha Datta Makhija for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR lodged on 5.3.1996 at 12.30 p.m., charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction upheld; High Court: Conviction upheld; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the two appellants, alongwith another accused, caused the death of PW11's uncle by assaulting him with sharp edged weapons. All the weapons allegedly used in the crime were recovered on the disclosure statements made by the appellants and the other accused. PW.8 conducted post-mortem on the body of the deceased and found three incised wounds on the body, one on the neck, one on the chest and another in the abdomen, all caused by sharp edged weapons. PW11 testified to have witnessed the incident. The prosecution also emphasized that the FIR was lodged promptly and with all details, indicating the truth of the version.
defence_argument: The appellants challenged their conviction on grounds that the ocular evidence was contradictory to the medical evidence as regards the time of death, and that the alleged eye witness PW.11 was closely related to the victim and none of the independent witnesses examined by the prosecution supported its case to the extent that PW.11 could be present on the place of occurrence at the relevant time.
legal_principle_applied: The ocular evidence would have primacy unless it is established that oral evidence is totally irreconcilable with the medical evidence. Where the medical evidence goes so far that it completely rules out all possibility of the ocular evidence if proved, the ocular evidence may be disbelieved.
precedent_relied_upon: State of U.P. v. Hari Chand (2009) 13 SCC 542; Abdul Sayeed v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2010) 10 SCC 259; Bhajan Singh @ Harbhajan Singh & Ors. v. State of Haryana, (2011) 7 SCC 421; Mangu Khan & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan AIR 2005 SC 1912; Baso Prasad & Ors. v. State of Bihar AIR 2007 SC 1019; Kartik Malhar v. State of Bihar (1996) 1 SCC 614; Himanshu @ Chintu v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2011) 2 sec 36; Manju Ram Kalita v. State of Assam (2009) 13 SCC 330; Leela Ram (Dead) thr. Duli Chand v. State of Haryana & Anr. (1999) 9 SCC 525
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because it is improbable that the appellants had been enroped falsely as promptness in lodging the FIR showed that there was no time for manipulation. Prompt and early reporting of the occurrence by the informant with all its vivid details gives an assurance regarding truth of its version.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution case was that two appellants, along with another accused, caused the death of the victim by assaulting him with sharp edged weapons. The victim was taken to the hospital where he was examined by a doctor and declared dead. The accused were arrested, and the weapons used in the crime were recovered on their disclosure statements. The trial court convicted the two appellants under Section 302 IPC and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for life. The conviction was upheld by the High Court. The appellants challenged their conviction on the grounds that the ocular evidence was contradictory to the medical evidence regarding the time of death and that the alleged eye witness was closely related to the victim. The Supreme Court held that the ocular evidence had primacy unless it was established that oral evidence was totally irreconcilable with the medical evidence. The Court also noted that the witness's testimony was trustworthy and that the prosecution case was supported by other evidence, including the statements of the Investigating Officer and the recovery of weapons.

title: JAGGA SINGH AND ANR.  versus STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: JAGGA SINGH AND ANR. v. STATE OF PUNJAB
neutral_facts: The prosecution case is that three accused approached the house of Raja Singh. One of them fired at Baggar Singh, hitting him on the right thigh, causing him to fall. The accused then took Hoshiar Singh, another individual, away towards a village. Approximately 20 minutes later, the sound of three or four gunshots was heard. physical_harm: Lacerated wounds on the second victim, no gunshot wound
number_of_offences: Three offences charged, two counts finally upheld (Section 302 and 325 IPC)
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that a gun shot was fired at Baggar Singh which hit him in the leg, and that the post mortem report showed only lacerated wounds on the dead body of Hoshiar Singh with no gun shot wound.
witness_credibility: The court expressed doubt regarding the prosecution's version of events concerning the charge under Section 302 IPC, indicating some credibility issues with the prosecution's narrative.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 24.4.92; Trial judgment: 4.12.2006; High Court decision: 4.12.2006; Supreme Court decision: 03.02.2011
legal_representation: Rajiv Garg, Ashish Garg and Annam D.N. Rao for the Appellant; Kuldip Singh for the Respondent
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Section 307 IPC; High Court: Conviction under Section 302 IPC; Supreme Court: Acquitted under Section 302 IPC, convicted under Section 325 IPC read with Section 34 IPC
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that Hoshiar Singh was taken away by the accused and after 15/20 minutes gun shots were heard, leading to his death. They sought conviction under Section 302 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the post mortem report showed only lacerated wounds on the dead body of Hoshiar Singh, with no gun shot wound, creating doubt about the charge under Section 302 IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the principle of the benefit of doubt to the accused in the absence of conclusive evidence of the charge under Section 302 IPC.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the appellants were found guilty under Section 325 IPC read with Section 34 IPC for firing a gunshot at Baggar Singh which hit him in the leg.

neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution case is that three accused approached the house of Raja Singh. One of them fired at Baggar Singh, hitting him on the right thigh, causing him to fall. The accused then took Hoshiar Singh, another individual, away towards a village. Approximately 20 minutes later, the sound of three or four gunshots was heard. The next morning, the dead body of Hoshiar Singh was found. The post mortem report indicated that the deceased had only lacerated wounds, with no gunshot wounds present. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 307 IPC, while the High Court convicted them under Section 302 IPC. However, the Supreme Court found that the prosecution's case regarding the charge under Section 302 IPC was uncertain due to the absence of gunshot wounds on the deceased's body, leading to the acquittal of the accused on that charge.

title: KILAKKATHA PARAMBATH SASI & ORS. versus STATE OF KERALA
case_title: KILAKKATHA PARAMBATH SASI & ORS. v. STATE OF KERALA
neutral_facts: The accused, who were part of an unlawful assembly, assaulted the victim and his brother at a bus stand due to political animosity. The victim sustained grievous injuries and later died in the hospital. The prosecution presented evidence from multiple witnesses, including the victim's brother, who described the incident and the weapons used. The victim's brother was examined by a doctor who found multiple incised wounds on him. The deceased's body was subjected to a post-mortem, which revealed 58 injuries, most of which were incised and cutting wounds. The accused were charged with offenses under Sections 147, 148, 307, 324, and 302 of the IPC.
physical_harm: PW-1 was grievously injured with three incised wounds, and his brother died from 58 injuries, most of them incised and cutting wounds
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 147, 148, 307, 324 and 302 read with Section 149; four accused were finally upheld
motive: Political animosity between the Congress Party and the Bhartiya Janta Party
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the prosecution story as entirely correct and supported by the evidence of PW-2 and two independent witnesses (PWs 3 and 4).
witness_credibility: PW-1 is an injured witness and his presence cannot be disputed. The court found it difficult to believe that PW-1 would have left out the true assailants of his brother. The court also found the presence of PW-2, PW-3, and PW-4 to be credible despite their absence from the FIR.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 24th March 1994; Trial judgment: 23.05.2003; High Court decision: 23.05.2003; Supreme Court decision: 24 February 2011
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: U.R. Lalit, E.M.S. Anam, Fazlin Anam; Counsel for the State: Dinesh Dwivedi, G. Prakash, Beena Prakash, V. Senthil
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Reversed acquittal of four accused; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused persons belonged to the Bhartiya Janta Party and that due to political animosity, they formed an unlawful assembly and assaulted PW-1 and his brother with weapons, resulting in the brother's death. The prosecution story was fully supported by the evidence of PW-2 and two independent witnesses (PWs 3 and 4).
defence_argument: The defence argued that the facts of the case did not justify interference by the High Court in an appeal against acquittal. They contended that the Trial Court's findings were not perverse and that the prosecution story was not credible, with doubts about the presence and reliability of the witnesses.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the High Court should not interfere in an appeal against acquittal save in exceptional cases, and that interference is called for only if the findings of the Trial Court are not borne out by the evidence and are perverse.
precedent_relied_upon: Arulvelu and Anr. v. State represented by the Public Prosecutor and Anr. (2009 (10) SCC 206]
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court found the Trial Court's acquittal to be perverse, and the prosecution story was entirely correct and supported by the evidence of the witnesses.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who were part of an unlawful assembly, assaulted the victim and his brother at a bus stand due to political animosity. The victim sustained grievous injuries and later died in the hospital. The prosecution presented evidence from multiple witnesses, including the victim's brother, who described the incident and the weapons used. The victim's brother was examined by a doctor who found multiple incised wounds on him. The deceased's body was subjected to a post-mortem, which revealed 58 injuries, most of which were incised and cutting wounds. The accused were charged with offenses under Sections 147, 148, 307, 324, and 302 of the IPC. The trial court acquitted all accused, but the High Court reversed the acquittal of four accused, finding the trial court's decision to be perverse. The High Court endorsed the spontaneity of the FIR and found the prosecution's story to be supported by the evidence of multiple witnesses.

title: BHAIYAMIYAN @ JARDAR KHAN & ANR. versus STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH

title: GURMAIL SINGH versus STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: Gurmail Singh v. State of Punjab

title: ACHHAR SINGH versus STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH

key_evidence_accepted: The High Court accepted the consistent evidence against some of the accused which were overlooked by the trial court amid the chaos in evidence, and on basis of the evidence, convicted one accused u/s. 302 IPC and other u/ss. 326 and 323 IPC.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible and consistent, noting that their statements were corroborated by medical evidence and that the trial court erred in overlooking the credible and consistent evidence while proceeding with a baseless premise that the exaggerated statements made by the eye-witnesses belie their version.

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that every person is presumed innocent until proven guilty, and that the High Court has the power to re-appreciate evidence in an appeal against acquittal if the trial court's findings are perverse.

title: PARUBAI versus THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA

neutral_facts: The accused, Parubai, was living in a house with her husband, Gulab, and his first wife, Mandabai, along with their children. Parubai exited the house unscathed, while Mandabai and her daughter, Nikita, were burned and later died from their injuries. Their son, Akash, died in the fire. The father-in-law of Parubai, Gajanan, reported the incident and implicated Parubai. The prosecution argued that Parubai had a motive due to her second marriage and the arrangement for maintenance in favor of Mandabai.
physical_harm: Two children died due to burn injuries; first wife also suffered burn injuries
number_of_offences: Three counts charged; two counts upheld
premeditation_planning: Court found no premeditation or planning
key_evidence_accepted: The presence of kerosene residues on the frock of deceased Nikita and the recovery of a can smelling of kerosene were considered, but the court found these insufficient to establish the appellant's guilt without additional circumstantial links.
witness_credibility: The court disbelieved the evidence of PW-1 (the father-in-law) and the extra-judicial confession, considering them unreliable. The dying declarations were also disbelieved by the trial court and approved by the High Court as not trustworthy.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 02.08.2006; Trial judgment: 16.11.2007; High Court decision: 12.10.2017; Supreme Court decision: 10.08.2021

defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to establish a complete chain of circumstances to prove the appellant's guilt, and that the absence of injuries alone cannot be used to infer guilt. They also highlighted that the presence of kerosene in the house was common and not exclusive to the appellant.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that for conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of circumstances must be established so completely that it leaves no reasonable doubt, and the evidence must lead to the conclusion that it 'must be true' and not 'may be true'.
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; Devilal v. State of Rajasthan (2019) 19 SCC 447
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered the natural human reaction to flee from a fire, the lack of direct evidence linking the appellant to the fire, and the absence of a complete chain of circumstances pointing to her guilt.

defence_argument: The appellant's counsel argued that the appellant has been in jail without a charge-sheet being filed against him for over nine years, that he is a Chartered Accountant offering professional services within the framework of law, and that there is nothing in the prosecution complaint to show that he is in possession of 'the proceeds of crime'.

The company discovered that the accused had misappropriated the balance amount by forging signatures with the help of pledged documents. The Enforcement Directorate filed a prosecution complaint under the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002, alleging that the accused were involved in money-laundering. title: SANDEEP versus STATE OF UTTARAKHAND

physical_harm: Death caused by gunshot injuries
number_of_offences: Four offences charged, one upheld

witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their depositions corroborated the materials recovered from the scene of crime and the FIR, and that the presence of the other accused with weapons was not proved.

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence affirmed; High Court: Dismissed appeal and affirmed judgment; Supreme Court: Partly allowed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant shot the deceased, and the charge of murder framed against him was proved beyond doubt. The evidence of P.W.1 and P.W.2, along with material objects recovered from the scene, supported the prosecution's case.

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that even with minor discrepancies in the evidence, the prosecution's case can still be sustained if the core facts are established. It also emphasized the principle of proportionality in sentencing.

other_sentence_order: The appellant was required to pay the fine amount imposed by the Sessions Court if not already paid. The bail bond executed by the appellant was discharged.

title: STATE OF HARYANA versus MOHD. YUNUS & ORS.
case_title: State of Haryana v. Mohd. Yunus & Ors.
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Sections 302 and 323 read with Section 34 IPC
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim were strangers. The incident occurred when the accused approached the victim and others to teach a lesson after a previous fight. The victim sustained multiple injuries to his head, including incised wounds and bone-deep cuts. The accused were armed with weapons such as a lathi, kulhari, and pharsa. The victim died as a result of the injuries. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence to establish the incident. However, the credibility of the eyewitnesses was questioned due to contradictions in their statements and the presence of previous enmity between the parties. The recovery of weapons from the accused was not fully established, and the statements of the witnesses were found to be inconsistent and unreliable.
physical_harm: Injuries resulting in death and injuries to the informant, his son and another eye-witness
number_of_offences: Four offences/counts charged; two finally upheld (A2 convicted under Sections 302 and 323, A1 convicted under Section 323)
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the recovery of weapons from A1 and A2 was not proved, and the statements of the prosecution witnesses were contradictory, twisted, and improved, thus not reliable for conviction under Section 302 IPC.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as untrustworthy due to their contradictory statements, twisting of facts, and improvements made, which cast serious doubt on their credibility.
bail_history: Appellant-Mohd. Jamil (A2) is on bail during the pendency of this appeal
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 09.01.1999; Trial judgment: 25.07.2001; High Court decision: 26.10.2009; Supreme Court decision: 12 January 2024
legal_representation: P. N. Puri, Rahul Sharma, Mrs. Reeta Dewan Puri, Ravinder Pratap Singh, Manish Dhingra, Ayush Bhatia, Dr. Monika Gusain, Ashok Mathur, Advs. for the appearing parties
investigation_status: FIR registered on 09.01.1999; charge sheet filed on 01.04.2003; trial completed

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the conviction of Mohd. Jamil (A2) under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC is based on unimpeachable evidence and that the High Court ought not to have acquitted Mohd. Yunus (A1) of the charge under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the FIR is ante-timed and delayed, the conviction is based on the testimony of interested witnesses, and the presence of the informant (PW-1) is doubtful. They also pointed out contradictions and omissions in the statements of the prosecution witnesses.
legal_principle_applied: For trial under Section 302 IPC, if a witness is branded as untrustworthy having allegedly twisted the facts and made contrary statements, it is not safe to impose conviction on the basis of such witness's statement. When there is an effort to falsely implicate one accused person, the statement of such an eyewitness cannot be relied upon without strong corroboration.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the conviction of Mohd. Jamil (A2) under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC was set aside due to unreliable witness statements, but his conviction under Section 323 read with Section 34 IPC was maintained.

title: MARIAM FASIHUDDIN & ANR. versus STATE BY ADUGODI POLICE STATION & ANR.
respondent: STATE BY ADUGODI POLICE STATION & ANR.
case_title: Mariam Fasihuddin & Anr. v. State by Adugodi Police Station & Anr.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.420, s.468, s.471, s.34; Passports Act s.12(b)
trial_court_outcome: Chargesheet filed, case proceeded to trial
neutral_facts: The accused, a married couple, were alleged to have forged the signature of the husband on a passport application for their minor child. The husband, who was living abroad, had allegedly abandoned the wife and child in India. The wife sought to obtain a passport for the child, and the husband later filed a complaint alleging forgery. The Court quashed the FIR and all related proceedings, finding that the allegations did not meet the necessary legal standards for the charges brought against the accused.
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Charged with multiple offences under Sections 420, 468, 471 IPC and Section 12(b) of the Passports Act, 1967; however, the High Court and Trial Magistrate's orders were set aside
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the State FSL report explicitly stated that the alleged forgery of Respondent No. 2’s signatures on the passport application was inconclusive.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the motivations of the appellants were not rooted in deceit and that the grant of the passport to the minor child did not result in any loss or damage to respondent no. 2.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 02.06.2008 (child's birth), 07.04.2010 (complaint filed), 13.05.2010 (complaint lodged by respondent no. 2), 15.03.2018 (trial magistrate's order), 18.02.2021 (high court's order), 22 January 2024 (supreme court's judgment)
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Ranbir Singh Yadav, Mohammed Sharookh, Prateek Yadav, Ms. Anzu K. Varkey, Ms. Mahesh Sharma, Ms. Chembugari Abheeshna. Counsel for the State: Narendra Hodda, Sr. Adv., Sanchit Garga, R. D. Singh, Ms. Mithu Jain, Kunal Rana, Pranshu Kaushal

defence_argument: The defence argued that the actions of the appellants did not constitute deceit or damage, as the passport was obtained for the minor child's benefit and not at the cost of respondent No. 2. title: RAM SINGH versus THE STATE OF U.P.
case_title: Ram Singh v. The State of U.P.
aggravating_circumstances: Non-recovery of weapon, non-examination of ballistic expert
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.301/302 and s.307 IPC
neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused, Ram Singh, and another accused, Lala Ram, were involved in a fatal shooting incident. The victim, Dulli, was sitting on a cot in the courtyard of the accused's house. PW-1, the son of the deceased, and his brother Desh Raj were also present. According to the prosecution, Lala Ram instigated Ram Singh to fire at PW-1, but the bullet struck Dulli, causing her death. The police recovered some cartridges and pellets from the scene and the victim's body, but the weapon used was not recovered. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence, but there were inconsistencies in the testimonies of the witnesses.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment / Rigorous imprisonment for five years
physical_harm: Gunshot injury resulting in death
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged; both upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution failed to recover the weapon of crime, obtain a ballistic opinion, and examine a ballistic expert, which significantly weakened the prosecution's case.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses' evidence as suffering from serious lacunae and could not be said to be credible.
trial_duration: Trial judgment: 05.02.2018; High Court decision: 05.02.2018; Supreme Court decision: 21 February 2024
legal_representation: Pradeep Kumar Mathur, Chiranjeev Johri, Chandra Nand Jha, M.K. Tiwari, Sitesh Kumar, Arvind Kumar, Advs. for the Appellant; Rana Mukherjee, Sr. Adv., Samarth Mohanty, Ankit Goel, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Non-recovery of the weapon of crime, non-examination of ballistic expert, non-obtaining of ballistic opinion
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence imposed; High Court: Conviction and sentence confirmed; Supreme Court: Conviction and sentence set aside
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant Ram Singh was responsible for the death of the deceased, Dulli, by firing a shot from a country made pistol at her. They relied on the testimony of PW-1, the son of the deceased, and other witnesses, including the police investigation and post-mortem report. The prosecution claimed that the evidence, including the eyewitness accounts, was sufficient to prove the appellant's guilt beyond all reasonable doubt.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case was flawed due to glaring inconsistencies in the eyewitness accounts, the non-recovery of the weapon of crime, and the failure to obtain a ballistic report or examine a ballistic expert. They contended that the evidence was not credible and that the trial court and High Court erred in convicting the appellant while acquitting the co-accused Lala Ram on the same set of evidence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that non-recovery of the weapon of crime and non-examination of a ballistic expert do not automatically invalidate the prosecution's case, but if the evidence suffers from glaring inconsistencies and material witnesses are not examined, the omission may be fatal to the prosecution's case. The court also emphasized the principle of parity, stating that similar evidence against two accused cannot result in one being convicted and the other acquitted.
precedent_relied_upon: Javed Shaukat Ali Qureshi Vs. State of Gujarat, [2023] 12 SCR 220 : (2023) 9 SCC 164; Munna Lal Vs. State of U.P., [2023] 3 SCR 224 : (2023) SCC Online SC 80; Gurucharan Singh Vs. State of Punjab, [1963] 3 SCR 585 : AIR 1963 SC 340; Sukhwant Singh Vs. State of Punjab, [1995] 2 SCR 1190 : (1995) 3 SCC 367; State of Punjab Vs. Jugraj Singh, [2002] 1 SCR 998 : (2002) 3 SCC 234; Gulab Vs. State of U.P., [2021] 9 SCR 678 : (2022) 12 SCC 677; Pritinder Singh Vs. State of Punjab, [2023] 10 SCR 1033 : (2023) 7 SCC 727
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's guilt beyond all reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court found the evidence to be inconsistent and not credible, and the non-recovery of the weapon, non-examination of the ballistic expert, and failure to examine material witnesses rendered the prosecution's case insufficient to justify conviction.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution alleged that the accused, Ram Singh, and another accused, Lala Ram, were involved in a fatal shooting incident. The victim, Dulli, was sitting on a cot in the courtyard of the accused's house. PW-1, the son of the deceased, and his brother Desh Raj were also present. According to the prosecution, Lala Ram instigated Ram Singh to fire at PW-1, but the bullet struck Dulli, causing her death. The police recovered some cartridges and pellets from the scene and the victim's body, but the weapon used was not recovered. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence, but there were inconsistencies in the testimonies of the witnesses. The trial court acquitted Lala Ram, while convicting Ram Singh. The High Court upheld the conviction, but the Supreme Court found the evidence insufficient and overturned the conviction.

title: CHANDAN versus THE STATE (DELHI ADMN.)

neutral_facts: The accused and the victim were walking together when the accused stabbed the victim multiple times with a knife. The victim fell to the ground and later died at a hospital. Forensic evidence confirmed that the victim's blood was found on the knife, and the injuries sustained by the victim were consistent with the weapon used. witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as reliable, noting that the eye-witness (PW-2) was not discredited despite lengthy cross-examination by the defence.
post_offence_conduct: The accused was caught the same day in the vicinity along with the knife used in the commission of the crime.

title: ROHINI SUDARSHAN GANGURDE versus THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA & ANR.
case_title: Rohini Sudarshan Gangurde v. The State of Maharashtra & Anr.
neutral_facts: The accused, the wife of the deceased, was charged with abetment of suicide under Section 306 of the IPC. The deceased was found hanging in his home, and the mother of the deceased filed a complaint alleging harassment and abuse by the accused. The deceased had a child with the accused, and they had jointly purchased a house where they resided. The deceased was employed at a hospital. sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the Court found that the appellant had no intention to kill the deceased and did not give him a blow with the intention to kill or with knowledge that it was likely to cause death. other_sentence_order: The appellant was awarded rigorous imprisonment for a period of 10 years and a fine of Rs. 20,000/-. In default of payment of fine, the accused shall undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution case was that the deceased had a dispute with his brother over a residential house. On the date of the incident, the deceased, his wife, and his daughters were present in the house. The accused persons, including the brother of the deceased and the appellant, entered the house. The appellant was holding an iron rod and inflicted a blow on the head of the deceased. The brother of the deceased gave a lathi blow on other parts of the body of the deceased. Other accused also inflicted lathi blows on the deceased's back. Injuries were also inflicted on the deceased's wife. The accused persons then ran away. The injured were taken to the hospital. trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to death
neutral_facts: The accused, who was married and had one son aged about 20 years and two daughters aged 22 years and 13 years respectively, killed his wife and three children by pouring petrol on their persons and setting them on fire. The incident occurred 25-27 years after the marriage. The accused was last seen with his wife at about midnight and was in fact quarreling with her at that time. The incident happened at 4 or 4.30 a.m., with a time gap of about 4 hours between the last seen time and the incident. The accused was found with cash of Rs.7,68,080/- and several items of clothing, but his alibi was deemed false. A 10-litre white plastic can with petrol was found at the scene, indicating the accused had brought petrol to the scene. The accused was found with a red bucket used for pouring petrol on the victims, which was confirmed by a chemical analysis. The prosecution's case relied on circumstantial evidence, including the presence of the accused at the scene, the petrol can, and the absence of any other plausible explanation for the crime.

title: ALAMELU & ANR. versus STATE REPRESENTED BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE
respondent: STATE REPRESENTED BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE
case_title: Alamelu & Anr. v. State Represented by Inspector of Police
statutory_provisions: IPC s.366, s.376 read with s.109
neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that PW-2, the daughter of PW-1, was abducted and subjected to forcible marriage and rape by A-1 and others. The accused were charged under Sections 366 and 376 of the IPC. The victim's account of the abduction and marriage was questioned, with the court noting that she did not protest or seek help despite having opportunities to do so. The court also highlighted the lack of reliable evidence to confirm the victim's age and the absence of corroboration for her testimony.
physical_harm: Rape and sexual intercourse
number_of_offences: 8 counts charged, 8 counts upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The entire story about the abduction by car and the forced marriage was seemingly concocted. Even after the alleged marriage with A-1, PW-2 continued to be a willing partner in the entire episode. She did not protest nor made any complaint though she had the opportunity to do so on many occasions. The conduct of PW-2 from the time of her alleged abduction till the time of her alleged recovery was not natural for a girl who had been compelled to marry and subjected to illicit sexual intercourse.
witness_credibility: The testimony of PW-2 does not satisfy the test of being free from basic infirmities or improbabilities. The conduct of PW-2 and the inconsistencies in her testimony, along with the father's lack of involvement and the absence of reliable evidence regarding the transfer certificate, cast doubt on the credibility of the main witnesses.

legal_representation: Counsel for the accused and the State in the Supreme Court not specified
investigation_status: Charge-sheet filed against A-1 for offences punishable under Sections 366 and 376 IPC and accused Nos. 2 to 8 for offences punishable under Sections 366 and 376 read with Section 109 IPC
procedural_irregularity: The trial court as well as the High Court failed to take into consideration the inherent improbabilities in the case sought to be projected by the prosecution. The findings recorded by both the Courts below were perverse and unsupportable by the evidence on record.
appeal_history: The conviction of the accused-appellants was challenged on the ground that the conclusions reached by both the Courts below were perverse and that they ignored the inconsistencies and contradictions in the evidence of the witnesses. It was contended that the facts of the case clearly suggested that there was no question of any abduction, forcible marriage or rape. Per contra, the State contended that the prosecution version was consistent and further that, in exercise of its powers under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court normally does not interfere with the concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below and, thus, the instant appeals were liable to be dismissed. Allowance of the appeals, the Court held: Even though the powers of this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution are very wide, but in criminal appeals, this Court would not interfere with the concurrent findings of facts, save in very exceptional cases.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution alleged that PW-2 was abducted, forcibly married, and raped by A-1, with PW-2 being a minor at the relevant date. The prosecution version was consistent and sought to implicate the accused in the alleged abduction, forced marriage, and rape.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the entire story of abduction and forced marriage was concocted. precedent_relied_upon: Ramesh Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2001) 9 SCC 618; Thanu Ram v. State of Madhya Pradesh (Now Chhattisgarh) (2010) 10 SCC 353; K. Prema S. Rao and Anr. v. Yadla Srinivasa Rao and Ors. (2003) 1 SCC 217; Devi Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2007) 14 SCC 176
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court found the appellant guilty of abetment under Section 306 and cruelty under Section 498A of the IPC, based on the evidence that the deceased's suicide was instigated by the appellant.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was sentenced to 10 years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.10,000/-, in default to suffer further one year rigorous imprisonment for the offence under Section 306 of IPC. Evidence included the recovery of kerosene at the scene, statements from witnesses about the accused's behavior, and the pledging of the deceased's jewels. The trial court acquitted the accused, but the High Court reversed this decision, finding the prosecution's case credible. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, concluding that the deceased's suicide was instigated by the accused due to the cruelty and financial demands.

title: SURESH KUMAR versus STATE OF HARYANA

neutral_facts_raw: The accused was involved in an incident where five persons, including three children, died. The prosecution's case was based on circumstantial evidence, including the testimony of witnesses, an extra-judicial confession, and recovered incriminating items. The accused fled the scene and was later arrested. The post-mortem reports indicated the deaths were due to multiple injuries, and the evidence suggested the accused was responsible for the murders. The accused's conduct, including his false name during arrest and absence of a valid explanation for his actions, supported the prosecution's case. The courts below accepted the evidence as reliable and connected the accused to the crime.

title: INDRAJIT SURESHPRASAD BIND & ORS. versus STATE OF GUJARAT

neutral_facts: The accused, who were the husband and in-laws of the deceased, were alleged to have subjected the deceased to harassment and cruelty in connection with a demand for dowry, which led to her committing suicide by pouring kerosene on her body. The prosecution relied on a letter allegedly written by the deceased to her brother, which was the only evidence presented. However, there were doubts about the authenticity of the letter, as it was unclear whether it was written by the deceased or a man, and whether the deceased was at the location stated in the letter. key_evidence_accepted: The letter dated 16-02-2004 allegedly written by the deceased to her brother (PW-3) was the only evidence produced by the prosecution to prove that the appellants had subjected the victim to harassment and cruelty in connection with demand for dowry.
witness_credibility: The court expressed grave doubts about the authenticity of the letter written by the deceased to PW-3 and questioned the credibility of the evidence provided by PW-3, noting that he did not specifically state the deceased was at Ahmedabad on 16-02-2004.
bail_history: Appellants are on bail and their bail bonds are discharged
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 18-05-2004; Trial judgment: 04-12-2006; High Court decision: 04-12-2006; Supreme Court decision: 18-03-2013

defence_argument: The defence argued that the deceased was in Chaksiriya village with her brother's family in Bihar and was not at Ahmedabad on 16-02-2004, and that she committed suicide because she wanted to remain with her parents and not live with the appellants.

title: SUBODH NATH AND ANR. versus STATE OF TRIPURA
case_title: Subodh Nath and Anr. v. State of Tripura
neutral_facts: The accused, Subodh Nath and Paritosh, were prosecuted for the killing of Ashutosh. The prosecution case was supported by the testimony of an eyewitness, PW-13, who stated that the accused assaulted the deceased with an axe and a lathi, and that the accused later shot the deceased with a gun. PW-13 fled the scene due to fear of the accused. The evidence of PW-13 was corroborated by PW-6, who found the deceased and the accused grazing cows in the jungle. The Investigating Officer recovered an axe handle near the deceased's body.
offence_severity: Death caused by an axe and a gun, punishable under Section 302 IPC
physical_harm: Injuries on the dead body caused by an axe and a gun
number_of_offences: One offence charged, one upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of PW-13 is corroborated by the evidence of PW-6, the Investigating Officer (PW-19), and the inquest report (Ext. P-2), which show injuries on the deceased caused by an axe and a gun, and the recovery of the axe handle.
witness_credibility: The court found PW-13's evidence reliable despite discrepancies, noting that normal discrepancies in witness accounts are expected and do not automatically cast doubt on credibility unless they are material.
post_offence_conduct: PW-13 ran away from the place of occurrence due to fear of the appellants who had threatened him, but this was explained as a result of his fear and not as an indication of unreliability.
trial_duration: Offence: 09.10.1998; Trial judgment: 08.06.2005; High Court decision: 08.06.2005; Supreme Court decision: 19.03.2013
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Lalit Chauhan, Somanadri Goud, Kshatrashal Raj, Abhishek Vinod Deshmukh (for Parekh & Co.); Counsel for the State: Ritu Raj Biswas, Gopal Singh
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction upheld; High Court: Conviction upheld; Supreme Court: Appeal of appellant No.2 allowed, appeal of appellant No.1 dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused were guilty of the offence under Section 302/34 IPC, supported by the testimony of an eye-witness, PW-13, and corroborated by other evidence such as the recovery of the weapon and the inquest report. They also contended that the motive to kill was not established, but argued that direct evidence of the offence was sufficient.
defence_argument: The defence argued that appellant No.2 was below 18 years of age at the time of the offence and thus a juvenile under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, and that the 2000 Act should apply. They also claimed that the conviction of appellant No.1 was based on an unreliable sole witness, PW-13, who had run away from the scene and was a suspect, and that there were discrepancies in the evidence, lack of weapon recovery, and no established motive.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, applies to offences committed prior to its commencement if the accused was below 18 years of age at the time of the offence. It also emphasized that discrepancies in witness accounts are not sufficient to discard evidence unless they are 'material discrepancies' creating reasonable doubt.
precedent_relied_upon: Hari Ram v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2009) 13 SCC 211; State of Rajasthan v. Smt. Kalki and Anr. (1981) 2 SCC 752; Badri v. State of Rajasthan (1976) 1 SCC 442; Lallu Manjhi and Anr. v. State of Jharkhand AIR 2003 SC 854; Suresh Chandra Bahri v. State of Bihar AIR 1994 SC 2420
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the conviction that the accused were guilty of the offence under Section 302/34 IPC, with the court upholding the trial court's and High Court's conviction and sentence for appellant No.1, while remitting the case of appellant No.2 to the Juvenile Justice Board.
other_sentence_order: The case of appellant No.2 was remitted to the Juvenile Justice Board of North Tripura district for disposal in accordance with the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, Subodh Nath and Paritosh, were prosecuted for the killing of Ashutosh. The prosecution case was supported by the testimony of an eyewitness, PW-13, who stated that the accused assaulted the deceased with an axe and a lathi, and that the accused later shot the deceased with a gun. PW-13 fled the scene due to fear of the accused. The evidence of PW-13 was corroborated by PW-6, who found the deceased and the accused grazing cows in the jungle. The Investigating Officer recovered an axe handle near the deceased's body. The trial court convicted both accused under s.302/34 IPC, and the High Court upheld the conviction. However, the Supreme Court remitted the case of Paritosh to the Juvenile Justice Board as he was under 18 at the time of the offence, and acquitted Subodh Nath based on the corroborated evidence.

title: RAKESH AND ANOTHER versus STATE OF HARYANA

trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Sections 498-A and 302 read with Section 34 IPC

On the relevant date, her mother-in-law caught her hands, and her husband set her on fire with kerosene oil. The deceased was taken to the hospital, where she was examined by a doctor and a Judicial Magistrate recorded her dying declaration. offence_severity: Rigorous imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs.2000/- under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC
physical_harm: The deceased suffered burn injuries covering almost the entire body except the legs below the knees, with approximately 85% burns. She was also beaten up mercilessly by her husband before being set on fire.
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 498-A and 302 read with Section 34 IPC; both offences were upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found that the accused planned and executed the act of setting the deceased on fire with kerosene oil, indicating premeditation
motive: Harassment and cruelty due to dowry demands
key_evidence_accepted: The dying declaration of the deceased is fully acceptable since the Judicial Magistrate (PW-10) reached the hospital, satisfied herself through the statement of the duty doctor that the deceased was conscious and fit to make a statement, and recorded her statement in the form of question and answers.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, including the Judicial Magistrate and the duty doctor, as credible and reliable, noting that the deceased was fit to make a statement and that the procedure followed was proper.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 14.05.1998; Trial judgment: 27.09.2001; High Court decision: 15.05.2006; Supreme Court decision: 22.03.2013
legal_representation: R.N. Kush, S.K. Sabharwal for the Appellants; Kamal Mohari Gupta, Mohd. Zahid Hussain for the Respondent

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration is acceptable in view of the facts of the case and that the prosecution must establish its case beyond reasonable doubt.

title: BARKU BHAVRAO BHASKAR versus STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
case_title: Barku Bhavrao Bhaskar v. State of Maharashtra
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.34; Arms Act s.27
aggravating_circumstances: Motive for murder, blood stains on shirt, recovery of body at instance of accused
neutral_facts: The accused was the last person seen with the victim, a female child aged about 6 years. The victim was last seen with the accused at her residence. A child witness reported seeing the accused and the victim together. The accused led the authorities to the victim's body, which was found covered with stones and branches. The victim sustained severe head and ear injuries, and the post-mortem report indicated the injuries were antemortem. Bloodstains on the accused's shirt matched the victim's blood group. The accused had a motive for murder due to a dispute over wages. The accused made an extra-judicial confession admitting to the crime. The accused's shirt was recovered at his instance, and no injuries were found on his body, ruling out self-inflicted bloodstains. The accused was found to have led the authorities to the victim's body, which was covered with stones and branches.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment for Section 302 IPC, five years' rigorous imprisonment for Section 354 IPC, and three years rigorous imprisonment for Section 201 IPC
physical_harm: The deceased sustained bleeding injuries on her head and ear, along with abrasions and swelling, leading to cardio-respiratory arrest due to head injuries.
number_of_offences: The accused was prosecuted for offences under Sections 364, 302, and 201 IPC. The courts upheld all the charges.
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning as the motive for murder was established through evidence of a wage dispute.
motive: The motive for murder was the wage dispute between the appellant and PW-1, who had abused the appellant at the village.
key_evidence_accepted: Evidence of the doctor who conducted the post-mortem proved that the death was homicidal. The blood stains found on the appellant's shirt, considered along with the factum of the appellant having led the prosecution to discover his blood-stained clothes and the body of the deceased, could have been only that of the deceased.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of PW-3 (the mother of the deceased) and PW-7 (the shop owner) as reliable witnesses. The court also noted that the conduct of the child witness, who did not speak in court, was not found fault with and was held in favour of the prosecution.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 03.12.2000; Trial judgment: 10.02.2006; High Court decision: 10.02.2006; Supreme Court decision: 25.07.2013

defence_argument: The accused contended that there were doubts as to whether the death was homicidal and that the blood group of the accused was not tested to ascertain whether the blood stain on his shirt could be of his own blood.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the chain of circumstances against the accused was complete and that the death was homicidal based on the evidence of the post-mortem report.

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed due to the overwhelming evidence proving all the circumstances against the accused, including the homicidal nature of the death, the last seen theory, the blood-stained shirt, the recovery of the body, and the motive for murder.

title: SUNIL DAMODAR GAIKWAD versus STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
case_title: Sunil Damodar Gaikwad v. State of Maharashtra
aggravating_circumstances: Multiple deaths, use of sharp weapon
mitigating_circumstances: Poverty, no prior criminal record, attempt to commit suicide, remorse
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to death under s.302 and life imprisonment under s.307
neutral_facts: The accused, a tailor, assaulted his wife and two sons with a pair of scissors, causing their deaths, and inflicted stab injuries on his daughter. He left the daughter in a condition where she survived due to assistance from a neighbor. The accused then went to the police station and reported the incident. The prosecution relied on the daughter's testimony, medical evidence, and recovery of the weapon. The accused denied the allegations during his police statement but did not present any defense evidence.
offence_severity: Death (minimum/maximum: 302 IPC: death; 307 IPC: life imprisonment)
