number_of_offences: Two counts charged; both upheld
premeditation_planning: Not found; the act was a result of socio-economic compulsions and abject poverty
key_evidence_accepted: The appellant suffered from economic and psychic compulsions, including abject poverty, which led him to commit the murders. The key witness, PW1 (the daughter), provided a detailed and consistent account of the incident, corroborated by PW4 (the maternal aunt). The appellant's own statement to the police, where he explained his actions due to financial stress and family suffering, was also accepted as evidence.
witness_credibility: The main witnesses, particularly PW1 (the daughter) and PW4 (the maternal aunt), were found to be credible. Their accounts were consistent and corroborated each other, and PW1's testimony was further supported by medical evidence and the police statement.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant went to the police station and reported the incident, indicating cooperation with authorities. He also left the injured daughter in a condition where she could receive medical attention, showing some remorse and attempt to mitigate the consequences of his actions.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was delivered on 23.09.2010 by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, and the Supreme Court decision was on 10 September 2013.
legal_representation: Ramesh Chandra Mishra, Dr. Meera Agarwal for the Appellant; Sushil Karanjkar, Asha Gopalan Nair for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Convicted under Sections 302 and 307 IPC and sentenced to death under the first count and life imprisonment under the second one', 'high_court': 'Confirmed the death sentence and dismissed the appeal confirming the conviction and sentence under Section 307', 'supreme_court': 'Allowed the appeals in part, commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment under Section 302 and reduced the sentence under Section 307 to 7 years'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused caused the death of his wife and two sons and attempted to cause death of his daughter, and that the trial court's conviction and sentencing were appropriate.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the accused was suffering from economic and psychic compulsions due to abject poverty and that the case did not fall under the rarest of rare category, thus warranting a lesser sentence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that life imprisonment is the rule for murder, and death sentence is the exception, requiring special reasons to be recorded.
precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh vs. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684; Machhi Singh and Others vs. State of Punjab 1983 (3) SCR 413; Shankar Kisanrao Khade vs. State of Maharashtra (2013) 5 SCC 546; Ediga Anamma vs. State of Andhra Pradesh 1974 (3) SCR 329; Sushil Kumar vs. State of Punjab (2009) 10 SCC 434; Gopal Vinayak Godse vs. The State of Maharashtra and Others 1961 SCR 440
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the case did not fall under the rarest of rare category, and the 'individually inconclusive and cumulatively marginal facts and circumstances' tended towards awarding a lesser sentence of life imprisonment.
judicial_mitigating_factors: Economic and psychic compulsions, lack of prior criminal record, possibility of reforming and rehabilitating the accused, and the fact that the accused was not likely to be a menace or threat to society.
other_sentence_order: The death sentence under Section 302 was commuted to life imprisonment, and the life imprisonment under Section 307 was reduced to 7 years. If the life imprisonment is remitted or commuted to a specified period, the sentence under Section 307 shall commence thereafter.

title: RANJEET GOSWAMI versus STATE OF JHARKHAND & ANR.

evidence_type: School leaving certificate, testimony of head mistress
neutral_facts: The accused was charged with offences punishable under Sections 302 and 376 of the Indian Penal Code. To prove he was a juvenile at the time of the incident, he submitted a school leaving certificate issued by the Principal of a school. The certificate indicated his date of birth as 10.05.1991. The accused provided testimony from the Head Mistress of the school, who confirmed the authenticity of the certificate. The respondent contested the certificate, leading to an enquiry by the Juvenile Justice Board. The Board sought the opinion of a Medical Board, which opined the accused was approximately 20 years old at the time of the incident.
offence_severity: Sections 376, 302 and 201 of IPC: Minimum 7 years, Maximum 10 years (Section 302) and life imprisonment or death (Section 376)
physical_harm: Death caused
number_of_offences: Charged with 3 offences, 3 offences finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The school leaving certificate was accepted as it was proved by examining the Head Mistress of the school, who recognized the signature of the Principal who issued it, and the evidence was not challenged.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the Head Mistress's evidence as credible since her testimony was not challenged and she recognized the signature of the Principal who issued the school leaving certificate.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant surrendered before the court on 13.06.2008.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 12/13-04-2008; Trial judgment: 30.05.2009; High Court decision: 29.10.2010; Supreme Court decision: 18.09.2013

investigation_status: Charge sheet filed; application for age determination submitted; medical board opinion sought and accepted; case referred to Sessions Court; appeal filed and decided by High Court; appeal filed and decided by Supreme Court
appeal_history: Trial court: Case registered as Case No.132 of 2009; High Court: Criminal Revision No.504 of 2009 allowed, order of Sessions Judge set aside; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, order of Sessions Judge restored

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that if the school leaving certificate is properly proved, there is no need for a medical examination by a medical board, as laid down in Ashwani Kumar Saxena v. State of M.P.
precedent_relied_upon: Ashwani Kumar Saxena v. State of M.P. 2012 (10) SCR 540
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
neutral_facts_raw: The accused was charged with offences punishable under Sections 302 and 376 of the Indian Penal Code. title: RAJIB RANJAN & ORS. versus R. VIJAYKUMAR

neutral_facts: The Chhattisgarh State Electricity Board issued a tender for work at Hasedeo Thermal Power Station. title: NARESH KUMAR versus STATE OF HARYANA & ORS.
case_title: NARESH KUMAR v. STATE OF HARYANA
aggravating_circumstances: Demand of dowry soon before death, harassment, suicide by burning
neutral_facts: The accused, married to the deceased, was subjected to harassment for dowry by his family soon before her death. The prosecution presented evidence of the harassment, medical reports, and investigation findings. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the right to free legal aid is an essential ingredient of a fair trial and that the process of expediting criminal trials must not compromise the fundamental elements of fairness and the opportunity for the accused to prepare their defense.

A first information report (FIR) was lodged the next day by a village chowkidar, who was not an eyewitness. Two eyewitnesses testified about the incident, but their accounts were inconsistent with previous statements and lacked details about the severity of the assault. The body was found near a temple, 300 feet away from where the assault allegedly occurred. Medical evidence indicated severe injuries, including head trauma and rib fractures, suggesting a violent attack. witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (PW-2 and PW-6) as inconsistent and unreliable, noting that their testimonies did not corroborate each other and left significant gaps in the prosecution's story.

witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the main witnesses, including the injured witnesses and the medical examiner, and found their accounts to be consistent with the evidence and the post-mortem report.

The trial court acquitted both accused due to the hostility of key witnesses and the lack of corroboration for the dying declaration. The High Court, however, convicted Krishan based on the dying declaration, the statement of the Judicial Magistrate, and the Investigating Officer. The High Court emphasized that the dying declaration, when recorded properly, can form the basis of conviction if it is true and reliable.

title: RAJESH BHATNAGAR versus STATE OF UTTARAKHAND
case_title: Rajesh Bhatnagar v. State of Uttarakhand
aggravating_circumstances: Demand for dowry, cruel treatment, unnatural death, false defence
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Section 304-B IPC, sentenced to life imprisonment

The deceased was found dead in her matrimonial home, and the body was handed over to her family. The accused were found to have absconded after the body was handed over. witness_credibility: The statements of PW1 and PW2 were fully corroborated and found to be credible, with no contradiction or variation in their accounts.

title: KUNJUMON @ UNNI versus STATE OF KERALA
case_title: KUNJUMON @ UNNI v. STATE OF KERALA
aggravating_circumstances: Victim was a frail old lady; use of a wall clock to cause head injuries; resulting in her death
mitigating_circumstances: Appellant did not intend to kill the victim, but committed robbery
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced under s. 302, 397 and 449 IPC
high_court_outcome: Acquitted under s. 449, upheld conviction under s. 302 and 397
offence_finally_established: Murder, robbery, and causing grievous hurt
neutral_facts: The accused, along with another individual, entered the house of a victim and committed robbery. During the robbery, the accused dragged a frail elderly woman from her cot, beat her on the head with a wall clock, and robbed her of her jewelry. The victim succumbed to her injuries in the hospital several days after the incident. The prosecution presented evidence including eyewitness accounts, medical reports, and recovered stolen items. The accused was identified by the victim's daughter, who was a witness to the incident.
offence_severity: Death (Section 302) and Robbery (Section 397) - Minimum 7 years, Maximum Life Imprisonment
physical_harm: Injuries on head of a 90-year-old lady resulting in her death
number_of_offences: Three counts charged (Sections 302, 397, 449), two upheld (Sections 302 and 397)
premeditation_planning: The court found that the accused did not have premeditation for murder but had planned robbery
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of PW-2 (Lidiya), the 11-year-old daughter of the victim, was accepted by the court as credible due to her direct experience as a victim of the crime and the traumatic nature of the events. The court also relied on the medical evidence showing the victim's injuries were caused by the accused and the recovery of stolen items from the accused.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, particularly PW-2, as having higher credibility due to her status as a victim of the crime and the traumatic nature of the events. defence_argument: The defence argued that the absence of a Test Identification Parade (TIP) made the evidence of the victim unreliable. neutral_facts_raw: The accused, along with another individual, entered the house of a victim and committed robbery. title: VENKATESHA versus STATE OF KARNATAKA
case_title: Venkatesha v. State of Karnataka
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.307, s.427 rlw s.34; Explosive Substances Act s.3 rlw s.34 /PC
evidence_type: eyewitness, circumstantial, medical, recovery, dying declaration
aggravating_circumstances: Motive established, bomb planted with intention to kill
neutral_facts: The accused, along with another individual, planned to plant an explosive device at the shop of a victim with the intention to kill him. The bomb was placed in a cardboard box and left at the shop. When the box was opened, it exploded, resulting in the death of the victim and injuries to two other employees of the shop. The accused were tried for murder and other related offenses. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts, the testimony of an approver who was granted pardon, and forensic evidence to establish the case.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs.5,000/-, in default of payment, further simple imprisonment for three months; five years' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.1000/-, in default of payment, further simple imprisonment for one month; one year's rigorous imprisonment; ten years' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.2000/-
physical_harm: Death of one employee and injuries to two other employees
number_of_offences: Four offences/counts charged, three finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Yes, the court found premeditation/planning as the motive was established
motive: To kill PW-14 due to domestic troubles and interference in family affairs
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the prosecution case supported by the eye-witnesses, injured witnesses, and the approver's testimony, which was corroborated by oral depositions and forensic evidence.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, including the injured witnesses and the approver, and found no reason to discard their evidence despite the approver being a criminal.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 2nd April 1996; Trial judgment: 16.03.2004; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: January 8, 2013

The evidence of the approver PW-2 was corroborated by multiple witnesses and forensic evidence.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the conviction was based solely on the testimony of the approver PW-2 without sufficient corroboration, which they claimed made the conviction unsafe. They contended that the prosecution failed to establish the motive and the corroboration necessary to support the conviction.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the legal principle that while the testimony of an accomplice is admissible, it must be corroborated in material particulars by independent and credible evidence to support a conviction.
precedent_relied_upon: The court relied on the principle established in the Evidence Act, 1872, Section 133, and the established rule of practice that an approver's testimony must be corroborated.
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed due to the gravity of the offenses, including murder and causing grievous hurt, with the sentences for each offense being determined based on the severity of the crime and the intent to kill.

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the chain of circumstantial evidence was complete, no link was missing, and the accused had an opportunity to commit the murder. The courts below correctly held the accused guilty of the offences.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused and co-accused were seen with the victim on a specific date. The victim was later found dead in a canal. The body was recovered several days later, and a post-mortem was conducted. The medical report indicated the victim had sustained grievous injuries. Evidence included recovered items such as the victim's chappal, blood-stained clothing of the accused, and a blade with blood traces. title: DENY BORA versus STATE OF ASSAM

statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.34; Arms Act s.27
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302, acquitted under TADA

The deceased was shot from point blank range, as confirmed by the post mortem report. The prosecution relied on the testimony of a witness, PW-14, who came forward almost two years and eight months after the incident. The witness claimed to be threatened by the co-accused, but the delay in his statement and the lack of corroboration raised doubts about his reliability. The prosecution also failed to examine the deceased's wife and daughter, who were present at the scene and could have provided crucial evidence.
physical_harm: The deceased was shot dead in his clinic, resulting in homicidal death due to bullet injuries.
number_of_offences: The appellant was prosecuted for 8 offences, but only one was finally upheld.
key_evidence_accepted: The post mortem report confirming the deceased was shot from point blank range, establishing the death as homicidal.
witness_credibility: The court found the testimony of PW-14 (the sole eye-witness) to be thoroughly and wholly unreliable due to his delayed statement, lack of corroboration, and implausibility of his claim of being threatened.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was passed on 02.03.2013. The Supreme Court decision was on 27 August 2014.
legal_representation: P.K. Goswami, Vikas Singh for the appellant; Navnit Kumar, Corporate Law Group for the Respondent.

procedural_irregularity: Non-examination of material witnesses (wife and daughter of the deceased) which affected the prosecution case.
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Section 302 IPC. High Court: Acquitted under TADA but convicted under Section 302 IPC. Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction set aside.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased was shot dead by two unidentified youths from the point blank range, and that the accused-appellant was involved in the crime. defence_argument: The defence argued that the sole witness, PW-14, was unreliable due to his delayed statement and the lack of corroboration. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that conviction can be based on the testimony of a single witness provided he is wholly reliable, but if there are doubts about the testimony, the courts will insist on corroboration. sentencing_rationale: Not applicable

title: DHAN RAJ @ DHAND versus STATE OF HARYANA
case_title: Ohan Raj @ Dhand v. State of Haryana
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.341 and s.392 r/w s.397
confession: Extra judicial confession of co-accused, but not relied on

The accused were linked to the crime through the recovery of stolen items and statements from a co-accused. The co-accused initially named different accomplices in two confessional statements, creating inconsistencies. The recovery of items was questioned as they were common and not of significant value. There was no direct evidence placing the accused at the scene of the crime, and the presence of the accused near the crime scene was not corroborated by independent evidence.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 2000/- under s. 302 r/w s. 341 IPC and rigorous imprisonment for eight years and a fine of Rs. 1,000/- under s. 392 r/w s. 397 IPC
physical_harm: Injuries caused by a sharp-edged weapon resulting in death due to shock and haemorrhage from multiple injuries
number_of_offences: Three counts charged, two finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution's case was based on circumstantial evidence, which must form a complete chain of events to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. However, the court found that the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete and did not conclusively prove the guilt of the accused.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, including the recovery witness PW7, as not inspiring confidence. The court also noted that the statement of PW15, an interested witness, lacked corroborating evidence and independent support.
bail_history: Appellant in Criminal Appeal No.703/2011 is already out on bail granted by this Court; appellant in Criminal Appeal No.1410/2010 is directed to be set at liberty forthwith
trial_duration: Dates of offence: January 24, 1997; Trial judgment: September 25, 1999; High Court decision: February 26, 2010; Supreme Court decision: May 9, 2014

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that circumstantial evidence must form a complete unbroken chain of events, with each circumstance proved beyond reasonable doubt, and that the prosecution must establish only one inference leading to the guilt of the accused.

title: RAJU @ DEVENDRA CHOUBEY versus STATE OF CHHATISGARH
case_title: Raju @ Devendra Choubey v. State of Chhattisgarh
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Section 302 r/w Section 34 and Section 1208, IPC
neutral_facts: The prosecution case was that on 25.11.2003, the accused's husband returned home from a clinic and found a servant, aged 13 years, weeping. Upon entering the house, he discovered his daughter-in-law dead and his wife unconscious. The accused, who was the step mother-in-law of the deceased, had a domestic dispute with the deceased. The servant, who worked with the family, identified the accused persons in court. The servant stated that one accused caught the deceased and another attacked her with a knife 3-4 times. The incident occurred in the courtyard, with the accused present in the passage. The accused threatened the servant not to disclose the incident. The accused fled after the assault, and one of them took the servant to the terrace and instructed him to falsely accuse thieves.
offence_severity: Death (Section 302) with minimum/maximum punishment as per IPC
physical_harm: Incised wounds and internal injuries leading to neurogenic and hemorrhagic shock
number_of_offences: Four counts charged, three finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Yes, accused no. 1 caused the deceased to be killed and engaged accused no. 2 and 4 as contract killers
key_evidence_accepted: The deposition of PW-21, a 13-year-old servant brought by accused no. 1, was accepted as reliable. His statement that accused no. 2 attacked the deceased with a knife was corroborated by the recovery of the knife from accused no. 2. The court also noted that accused no. 1 had a scuffle with the deceased, as evidenced by her hair being found in her grip during investigation.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the child witness PW-21 as credible, noting that he had no motive to falsely implicate the accused, was taken care of by accused no. 1, and had no ulterior motive. His testimony was not discarded despite his association with the police, and his statement was corroborated by the recovery of the knife from accused no. 2.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was delivered on 17.09.2010 by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur, and the Supreme Court decision was on 21 August 2014.
legal_representation: For the Appellant: P.C. Agrawala, Dr. Rajesh Pandey, Mahesh Pandey, Priyanka Pandey, Mridula Ray Bhardwaj, Revathy Raghavan, Vidya Dhar Gaur; For the Respondent: Atul Jha, Sandeep Jha, Dharmendra Kumar Sinha
investigation_status: FIR registered on 25.11.2003, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Section 302 r/w Section 34 and Section 1208, IPC; High Court: Confirmed the conviction; Supreme Court: Dismissed the appeals of accused no. 1, 2 and 4 and allowed the appeal of accused no. 3
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that accused no. 1 hired contract killers accused no. 2 and 4 to kill her daughter-in-law (deceased) due to domestic disputes. The child witness PW-21, who was brought up by accused no. 1, provided testimony that accused no. 2 and 4 attacked the deceased with a knife, and the knife was recovered from accused no. 2. The prosecution also highlighted the motive of accused no. 1 to hinder the marriage of her son.
defence_argument: The defence argued that accused no. 3 (Mahesh) did not play any role in the crime, as there was no evidence of his involvement, no weapon or property connected with the crime was seized from him, and he was merely seen standing outside the house. The defence also questioned the reliability of the child witness PW-21, suggesting he might have been tutored by the police.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that common intention and conspiracy are matters of inference, and if any benefit of doubt arises, it must go to the accused. The Court also emphasized the need for corroboration of the testimony of a child witness in cases where the accused are strangers to the witness.
precedent_relied_upon: Subash and Shiv Kumar Vs. State of UP. (1987) 3 SCC 331; Mohd. Abdul Hafeez Vs. State of Andhra Pradesh AIR 1983 SC 367; Budhsen and Anr. Vs. State of UP. (1970) 2 SCC 128; Suresh Sakharam Nangare Vs. State of Maharashtra (2012) 9 SCC 249; Jai Bhagwan Vs. State of Haryana AIR 1999 SC 1083; Ramashish Yadav Vs. State of Bihar (1999) 8 SCC 555; Baliya v. State of M.P. (2012) 9 SCC 696
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed as the Court upheld the conviction of accused no. 1, 2, and 4 under Section 302 r/w Section 34 and 1208 of the IPC, considering the evidence of the child witness and the corroborating knife recovery. Accused no. 3 was acquitted due to lack of evidence of his involvement.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The Court considered that the child witness PW-21 was brought up by accused no. 1, who took care of him, sent him to school, and provided him with food and residence, which made it unlikely for him to falsely implicate anyone.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The Court noted that accused no. 2 and 4 had a single mission to kill the deceased, and there was no evidence of their previous animosity with the deceased, indicating a premeditated act.
other_sentence_order: The Court acquitted accused no. 3 and discharged his bail bonds and sureties. It also emphasized the need for corroboration of child witness testimony and the importance of fair identification procedures.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution case was that on 25.11.2003, the accused's husband returned home from a clinic and found a servant, aged 13 years, weeping. Upon entering the house, he discovered his daughter-in-law dead and his wife unconscious. The accused, who was the step mother-in-law of the deceased, had a domestic dispute with the deceased. The servant, who worked with the family, identified the accused persons in court. The servant stated that one accused caught the deceased and another attacked her with a knife 3-4 times. The incident occurred in the courtyard, with the accused present in the passage. The accused threatened the servant not to disclose the incident. The accused fled after the assault, and one of them took the servant to the terrace and instructed him to falsely accuse thieves. The prosecution examined 32 witnesses, and the trial court convicted all the accused under Section 302 r/w Section 34 and Section 1208, IPC. The High Court confirmed the conviction.

title: TANUA RABIDAS versus STATE OF ASSAM
case_title: Tanua Rabidas v. State of Assam
accused_occupation: Assistant in the Social Welfare Department
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment and fine of Rs.1,000/-
neutral_facts: The accused, along with a co-accused, were present in the house on the day of the incident. The accused poured kerosene oil on his wife and set her on fire. The victim was taken to the hospital where she succumbed to burn injuries. The victim's brother lodged an FIR. A dying declaration was made by the victim in the presence of a doctor and a nurse, stating that her husband had set her on fire. The doctor and nurse's statements were corroborated by the victim's brother and another witness who accompanied him to the hospital. The prosecution case relied on the dying declaration, medical evidence, and eyewitness accounts to establish the accused's guilt.
physical_harm: Burn injuries resulting in death
number_of_offences: Charged with 3 offences, 1 upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the dying declaration made by the victim to PW-6 (Dr. Langkumer) and PW-7 (Nabanita Barauh), which was corroborated by PW-1 and PW-8.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of PW-6 and PW-7 as reliable witnesses, noting they were not related to the victim, not interested witnesses, and their statements were fully corroborated by other witnesses.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: not stated; Trial judgment: 30.03.2006; High Court decision: 20.03.2007; Supreme Court decision: 04.09.2014
legal_representation: P.K. Goswami, Parthiv K. Goswami, A. Henry, Rajiv Mehta for the Appellant; Avijit Roy for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge sheet filed; trial completed

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant-accused poured kerosene oil on his wife and set her on fire, leading to her death. The evidence included two dying declarations from the victim, corroborated by witnesses, and the victim's death was attributed to burn injuries.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the dying declaration made by the victim was unreliable, as it was an oral statement and there was no smell of kerosene oil on the victim's body. They also cited the case of Surinder Kumar v. State of Haryana to challenge the admissibility of the dying declaration.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration is admissible if it is corroborated by other evidence and the circumstances surrounding its making are not suspicious.
precedent_relied_upon: Surinder Kumar v State of Haryana (2011) 10 SCC 173; State of Rajasthan vs. Kishore (1996) 8 SCR 217
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence of life imprisonment was imposed because the prosecution proved the case beyond all reasonable doubt, and the trial court and High Court found the appellant guilty under section 302 IPC.

title: KRISHIKA LULLA & ORS.  versus SHYAM VITHALRAO DEVKATIA & ANR.
case_title: KRISHIKA LULLA & ORS. v. SHYAM VITHALRAO DEVKATIA&ANR.
statutory_provisions: Copyright Act s.63; IPC s.406, s.420
neutral_facts: The accused, who were involved in a film production, faced a criminal complaint alleging infringement of copyright in the title of a story synopsis. The complainant claimed that the title 'Desi Boys' was used by the accused for their film titled 'Desi Boyz', which was released in 2011. The complainant alleged that the title was the soul of his story and that its use by the accused constituted infringement. The accused argued that the title was not a literary work and therefore not protected by copyright. The case involved a dispute over whether the title of a story could be considered a literary work under copyright law.
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Not stated
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the title 'Desi Boys' does not qualify as a 'literary work' under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957, and therefore, no copyright subsists in it.
witness_credibility: The court did not assess the credibility of the main witnesses as the case primarily revolved around legal interpretation of copyright law rather than witness testimony.
trial_duration: Dates of offence not stated, trial judgment dated 22.03.2012, High Court decision not stated, Supreme Court decision dated OCTOBER 15, 2015
legal_representation: Raju Ramachandran, Chirag M. Shroff, Bhaskar Das, Nitin Mishra, Mrs. Mitali Gupta, Vikram Aditya Narayan, Advs. for the Appellants; Ramsuresh Vishwakarma, Rajiv Kumar Sinha, Dr. (Mrs.) Vipin Gupta, Kunal A. investigation_status: Process issued under Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957 read with Sections 406 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860

defence_argument: The defence argued that there is no copyright in the title of a story or film, and therefore, the criminal complaint under Section 63 of the Copyright Act is not tenable.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a title of a work, by itself, is not a subject of copyright and that copyright subsists only in original literary works as defined under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957.

Maxwell (1866-67) L.R.2 Ch. App. 307; Macmillan v. Suresh Chander Deb ILR 17 Cat 951; Longman v. Winchester (1809)16 Ves 269; Dicks v. Yates (1881) 18 Ch D 79
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable

The complainant alleged that the title was the soul of his story and that its use by the accused constituted infringement. title: AMRUTLAL LILADHARBHAI KOTAK & ORS. versus STATE OF GUJARAT
case_title: Amrutlal Liladharbhai Kotak & Ors. v. State of Gujarat
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Sections 304-B and 498-A of the IPC
neutral_facts: The accused, who were the husband and relatives of the husband of the deceased, were involved in a case where the deceased committed suicide. The deceased was married to one of the accused, and after the marriage, she was subjected to mental torture and harassment due to insufficient dowry. The deceased's father received a call informing him of the incident and arrived at the scene. The police registered a complaint against the accused, and the accused were arrested. During the trial, several witnesses testified about the mental torture and harassment the deceased faced.
offence_severity: Minimum 10 years, maximum life imprisonment or death
physical_harm: The deceased committed suicide, and there was mental torture and harassment leading to her death
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 498-A, 304-B and 306; finally upheld under Sections 498-A and 304-B
premeditation_planning: The court found that the accused subjected the deceased to cruelty, which led to her suicide
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of friends and relatives of the deceased regarding mental torture and harassment by the accused due to insufficient dowry, and the version of the witnesses PW-1, PW-7, PW-8 and PW-9.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their statements were supported by each other and established that the accused were greedy and had started demanding dowry from the date of marriage.
post_offence_conduct: The accused absconded for thirty six days and ultimately surrendered themselves at the Morbi City Police Station.
trial_duration: The trial was held in Sessions Case No.52/2000, with the complaint registered on 23.03.2000 and the trial judgment passed by the Trial Court. The High Court confirmed the order on 17.06.2009, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 26.02.2015.

defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to substantiate the guilt of the accused under Sections 304-B and 306 of the IPC, and that the evidence of relatives and friends of the deceased was not reliable and could not be solely relied upon.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that Sections 304-B and 498-A of the IPC are not mutually inclusive, and that a presumption under Section 113-A of the Evidence Act can be raised if certain foundational facts are established and the event occurred within seven years of marriage.

sentencing_rationale: Not applicable

title: STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH versus RAKESH MISHRA
case_title: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Rakesh Mishra
statutory_provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act s.13(2), s.13(1)(d); IPC s.120B
trial_court_outcome: Framing of charges against three accused
high_court_outcome: Set aside the order of framing charges
offence_finally_established: Criminal conspiracy, illegal gratification, and misuse of authority
neutral_facts: The accused, including Rakesh Mishra, were involved in granting building and completion certificates to a hotel and club without proper approvals. The original building permission was granted to the applicant, and later a revised plan was submitted. The revised plan involved significant changes from the original plan, including increased built-up area for the hotel and decreased for the club. The accused granted the revision without approval from any committee and accepted honorary membership in the club. The prosecution alleged that these actions constituted illegal gratification and misuse of authority.
offence_severity: Minimum 6 months to maximum 3 years of imprisonment
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Three offences/counts charged, all finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The revised building plan, which was a complete departure from the original plan, and the granting of the completion certificate merely 7 days after the revision of building permission, along with the acceptance of honorary membership, were accepted as key evidence.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses by examining the material before it against the prevailing law to reach its conclusions, without commenting on the credibility of specific witnesses.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: Not stated; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: 18.05.2007; Supreme Court decision: 23.03.2015
legal_representation: Arvind Varma, Deepika Shari, C. D. Singh for the Appellant; Sumit Kumar Sharma, Niraj Sharma, Brajesh Kumar for the Respondent

prosecution_argument: The State argued that the High Court traversed beyond the permissible limit while deciding the legality of the order framing charges, being a pre-trial stage, and that only the charge-sheet along with the accompanying material should be considered at the stage of framing of charges.
defence_argument: The defence argued that G.S. Jadon cannot be held liable for any act/omission done prior to or after his period of service as Building Officer, and that the revision jurisdiction of the High Court also includes the inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of Cr.PC.
legal_principle_applied: The Court applied the principle that only the charge-sheet along with the accompanying material is to be considered at the stage of framing of charges, so as to satisfy whether a prima facie case is made out, and that it has to be the subjective satisfaction of the Court framing charges.

The prosecution alleged that the accused and his brother murdered the wife, but the evidence did not directly link the accused to the act. Witnesses testified that they found the wife in a hanging posture and called for help, after which the accused and others arrived and cut the saree to bring down the body. The medical evidence did not conclusively establish the cause of death as homicidal hanging.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 10000/-
physical_harm: The deceased was found in a hanging posture with movements, and later declared dead
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged, one upheld
premeditation_planning: The court did not find premeditation/planning
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of witnesses when considered in conjunction with the testimony of the doctor does not link the appellant directly or indirectly with the actual act leading to the unnatural death of the deceased. The medical evidence also does not decisively establish the case to be of homicidal hanging.
witness_credibility: The courts found the testimony of DWI (Cheriyan @ Papputty) to be trustworthy, noting that he was a major with the required maturity in life's perspectives and would not have lied for the appellant, his father, only to see him through, though knowing him to be the real perpetrator of the crime.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 19.9.2000; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: 3 October 2016
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Basant R., Raghenth Basant, M. F. Philip, Kartik Ashok, Abhishek Tiwari (For Senthil Jagadcesan); Counsel for the State: G. Prakash, Jishnu M. L., Mrs. Priyanka Prakash, Mrs. Beena Prakash, Manu Srinath, Nishe Rajen Shonker
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction of appellant under Section 302 IPC; High Court: Sustained conviction; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant, along with his brother, murdered his wife by strangulating her with a plastic rope and then hanging her from a hook. They claimed that the appellant had resigned from his police service to move to Saudi Arabia with an extra-marital partner, thereby deserting his wife and children, and that the circumstantial evidence supported the charge of murder.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant was not present at the house when the deceased died, and that the medical evidence did not conclusively establish homicidal hanging. They also highlighted the acquittal of the co-accused and the lack of direct evidence linking the appellant to the crime, asserting that the prosecution's case was based on suspicion rather than proof.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that suspicion cannot replace proof in criminal cases, and that the prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The court emphasized that circumstantial evidence must be conclusive and leave no room for reasonable doubt in favor of the accused.
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; R. Rajendran Nair v. State of Kerala (1998) SCC (Crl.) 254; Sujit Biswas v. State of Assam (2013) 12 SCC 406; Dhan Raj @ Dhand v. State of Haryana (2014) 6 SCC 745
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed due to the conviction under Section 302 of the IPC for the murder of the appellant's wife, but the Supreme Court overturned this conviction due to insufficient evidence and reasonable doubt in the appellant's favor.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered the absence of direct evidence linking the appellant to the crime, the acquittal of the co-accused, and the lack of conclusive medical evidence supporting the prosecution's claim of homicidal hanging.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a police constable, and his brother were involved in an incident where the accused's wife was found hanging in their home. The prosecution alleged that the accused and his brother murdered the wife, but the evidence did not directly link the accused to the act. Witnesses testified that they found the wife in a hanging posture and called for help, after which the accused and others arrived and cut the saree to bring down the body. The medical evidence did not conclusively establish the cause of death as homicidal hanging. The accused and his brother were acquitted by the trial court and the High Court, with the Supreme Court affirming their acquittal due to the lack of conclusive evidence linking the accused to the crime.

title: SURESH SINGHAL versus STATE (DELHI ADMINISTRATION)
case_title: Suresh Singhal v. State (Delhi Administration)
mitigating_circumstances: Right to private defence, no premeditation
neutral_facts: The accused and the deceased were involved in a dispute over the sale of property. On the day of the incident, the accused and his father arrived at the office of a third party where the deceased and his brothers were already present. An altercation occurred between the accused and the deceased, leading to a scuffle. During the scuffle, the deceased and his brothers attempted to strangle the accused. The accused reached for his revolver, and upon seeing the gun, the deceased released him and started running. The accused then fired the shot, which hit the deceased from behind. The bullet entered the body below the right shoulder and traveled upwards without exiting. The medical evidence indicated that the shot was fired from a distant range, and there was no blackening or charring around the wound.
physical_harm: Two brothers died as a result of the shooting
number_of_offences: 7 counts charged, 2 counts upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found no premeditation or planning
key_evidence_accepted: Evidence proved that there was a scuffle in which the appellant was pinned to the floor and deceased attempted to strangulate the appellant. In the scuffle, appellant may have pulled out his gun and upon seeing the gun, the deceased may have released the appellant and started running upon which the appellant may have fired the shot which hit deceased on back. The shot was fired from a distant range, and the bullet entered the body below the right shoulder and travelled upwards without exiting.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses by noting that PW-3 (Hans Raj) did not specify that the appellant shot him, and that the version of PW-30 (Tarsem Kumar) was doubted due to the bullet entry wound being on the back of the deceased, not the front. The court also found that the testimony of PW-23 (Subhash Chand Mahajan) and PW-27 (Sarover Kumar) about the scuffle was unshaken in cross-examination.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was delivered on 01.09.2010 by the High Court of Delhi, and the Supreme Court decision was on 02.02.2017.
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: D Sushil Kumar, S. K. Aggarwal, Aditya Kumar, S. K. Sinha, Arun K. Sinha. Counsel for the State: P. K. Dey, R. K. Verma, Ms. Rashmi Malhotra, Ms. Sadhna Sandhu, B. K. Prasad, Ms. Reena Rai, Ms. Shreyasi Chakraborty, Manish, Mrs. Anil Katiyar.
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Sections 302 and 304 read with Section 34 of IPC. High Court: Conviction under Sections 302 and 304 read with Section 34 of IPC. Supreme Court: Conviction under Section 302 for murder of Kishan Lal is set aside, and conviction under Section 304 is maintained.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant shot the deceased and his brothers during a confrontation, resulting in their deaths, and that the appellant took undue advantage of the situation by using the gun even though the deceased and his brothers were unarmed.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant acted in self-defence, as he was being strangled by the deceased and his brothers during a scuffle, and that the shooting was a result of a sudden fight in the heat of passion, not premeditation.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a person in imminent and reasonable danger of losing their life or limb may use self-defence, even if it results in the death of the assailant, provided it is without premeditation and without taking undue advantage.
precedent_relied_upon: Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab and Another (2010) 2 SCC 333 : [2010] 1 SCR 642
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the appellant was already serving a sentence of 13 years, and the court sentenced him to the period already undergone under Section 304 of the IPC.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered that the appellant acted in self-defence without premeditation and that the shooting occurred in a sudden fight in the heat of passion.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused and the deceased were involved in a dispute over the sale of property. On the day of the incident, the accused and his father arrived at the office of a third party where the deceased and his brothers were already present. An altercation occurred between the accused and the deceased, leading to a scuffle. During the scuffle, the deceased and his brothers attempted to strangle the accused. The accused reached for his revolver, and upon seeing the gun, the deceased released him and started running. The accused then fired the shot, which hit the deceased from behind. The bullet entered the body below the right shoulder and traveled upwards without exiting. The medical evidence indicated that the shot was fired from a distant range, and there was no blackening or charring around the wound. The accused was convicted of murder, but the conviction was later overturned on the grounds that the accused acted in self-defense without premeditation.

title: S. SUBBULAXMI versus KUMARASAMY & ORS.
case_title: S. Subbulaxmi v. Kumarasamy & Ors.
aggravating_circumstances: Land dispute, family relationship, use of weapons
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim were closely related individuals involved in a land dispute. The victim, Subramani, was attacked by the accused during a confrontation over the land issue. The accused used an iron rod and cart twigs to assault the victim, resulting in his death. The victim's father was injured during the incident. The police recorded statements from witnesses and conducted an investigation, but the prosecution faced challenges in proving the guilt of the accused due to inconsistencies in the evidence and delays in reporting.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment for Section 302 IPC / Rigorous imprisonment for three years for Section 506(11) IPC
physical_harm: Deceased sustained six serious bleeding injuries on the scalp, and DW2 sustained multiple injuries including fractures and lacerations
number_of_offences: Three offences/counts charged, all finally upheld by the trial court but set aside by the High Court
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution story is not trustworthy and the evidence adduced on record is full of contradictions.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as unreliable, noting that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and that the evidence is full of contradictions.
trial_duration: The trial court passed the conviction order on 17th September, 1994. The High Court set aside the conviction on 22nd March, 2005. The Supreme Court judgment was delivered on 6th July, 2017.
legal_representation: Jayant Muth Raj, Ms. Malavika J., C. K. Sasi, Advs. for the Appellant; M. Karpaga Vinayagam, Sr. Adv., R. Nedumaran, S. Syed Mahaboob, M. Yogesh Kanna, Ms. Nithya, Ms. Maha Lakshmi, Partha Sarathi, Advs. for the Respondent.
investigation_status: Investigation in Crime No. 399/94 was continued for about three months and finally the proceedings were dropped by PW 11 - Inspector of Police for the reason that the accused in that case has already died on 15-09-1994.
procedural_irregularity: The High Court noted that the investigating agency ignored its paramount duty of bringing home the guilt of the accused with probable evidence as admissible under law, rather, spent time and mind on creating 'two occurrences and substantiating the same with the circumstances'.
appeal_history: The trial court convicted the accused. The High Court acquitted the accused. The Supreme Court upheld the acquittal of the accused.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused were guilty beyond reasonable doubt, citing the testimony of the eye witness, the recovery of weapons used, the chemical analyst's report, and the statements of the doctors. They also emphasized the place of occurrence, the injuries on DW2, and the forensic reports with regard to blood stains on material objects and weapons used by the accused.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case was fabricated, with the police creating two separate incidents and tampering with the FIR to create a wrong impression. They also contended that the deceased had raised violence upon DW2 and that the police had prevented the accused from taking the plea of self-defence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied judicial scrutiny to the facts and circumstances of the case, emphasizing that the prosecution must prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
precedent_relied_upon: Sadhu Saran Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. (2016) 4 SCC 357; Hare Krishna Singh & Ors. v. State of Bihar (1988) 2 SCC 95; Appabhai & Anr. v. State of Gujarat (1988) Suppl. SCC 241; State of Andhra Pradesh v. Punati Ramulu & Ors. AIR 1993 SC 2644; Ashish Batham v. State of MP. (2002) 7 SCC 317; Joginder Singh v. State of Haryana (2014) 11 SCC 335
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable

title: STATE OF HARYANA versus KRLSHAN & ANR.
case_title: State of Haryana v. Krishan & Anr.
aggravating_circumstances: Sale of poisonous liquor, attempt to destroy evidence
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of culpable homicide and other charges
neutral_facts: The prosecution case centered around a tragic incident where 36 persons died and 44 persons lost their eyesight after consuming spurious liquor purchased from a licensed liquor vend. Medical evidence confirmed that the cause of death and loss of vision was due to the consumption of liquor adulterated with methyl alcohol. Victims and their relatives stated they purchased the liquor from the respondents' vend, which was corroborated by the conduct of the respondents in disposing of remaining stock after the incident. The prosecution presented evidence showing the respondents were licensed vendors and that they had knowledge of the harmful effects of the liquor they sold.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs.10,000/- each for Section 302 IPC read with Section 120B IPC; imprisonment for a term of 5 years with fine of Rs.5,000/- each for Section 328 IPC read with Section 120B IPC
physical_harm: 36 persons lost their lives and 44 persons lost their eye sight due to consumption of poisonous liquor containing methyl alcohol
number_of_offences: 48 persons were arrayed as accused; 2 were convicted, others acquitted
premeditation_planning: Yes, the respondents were aware of the disastrous consequences of selling spurious liquor and planned to make quick money
key_evidence_accepted: Medical evidence supported the prosecution case that the cause of death and loss of eye sight was the result of consuming spurious liquor. The victims and their relatives stated that they purchased liquor from the vends of respondents. Conduct of the respondents in throwing away remaining stock after the incident came into limelight is also a supporting piece of evidence.
witness_credibility: Such contemporary statements of those very persons who suffered loss of eye-sight immediately after the incident cannot be ignored and there is no reason to disbelieve them. Such statements also become relevant under Section 7 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
post_offence_conduct: The respondents tried to destroy remaining bottles by throwing them away in the river/canal after the tragedy struck.
trial_duration: Offence: December 1, 1980; Trial judgment: August 18, 2000; High Court decision: May 09, 2006; Supreme Court decision: June 09, 2017
legal_representation: Sanjay Kumar Tyagi, Addi. AG, Dilip Pratap, Kamal Mohan Gupta, Advs. for the Appellant; R. S. Sodhi, Sr. Adv., Harpreet Singh Sandhu, Satyapal Khushal Chand Pasi, Ms. Apama Rohatgi Jain, Mahesh Kasana, S. K. Dhingra, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction of Krishan and Som Nath; High Court: Acquittal of respondents; Supreme Court: Conviction ordered by trial court is restored
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the respondents were responsible for selling spurious liquor containing methyl alcohol, which caused the deaths of 36 persons and blindness in 44 others. The medical evidence supported this claim, and the victims and their relatives stated they purchased the liquor from the respondents' vends. The respondents' attempt to destroy remaining bottles after the incident further supported their culpability.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was no evidence connecting the respondents to the consumption of methyl alcohol by the victims. They claimed the prosecution's case was based on faulty investigation and that the respondents were not directly involved in the preparation or sale of spurious liquor.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the presence of methyl alcohol in the victims' bodies, coupled with the victims' statements and the respondents' conduct, established their culpability under Section 300 IPC (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) and Section 120B IPC (conspiracy).
precedent_relied_upon: Joseph Kurian Philip Jose v. State of Kerala [1994] 4 Suppl. SCR 122 : (1994) 6 SCC 535; Fakhruddin v. State of MP. AIR 1967 SC 1326
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution proved the respondents' culpability in selling spurious liquor containing methyl alcohol, which caused the deaths and blindness of numerous victims. The respondents' conduct, including their attempt to destroy evidence, demonstrated full knowledge of the dangerous consequences of their actions.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The court weighed the respondents' greed and exploitation of vulnerable villagers, their full knowledge of the dangerous nature of the methyl alcohol, and their attempt to destroy evidence after the tragedy.
other_sentence_order: The High Court had directed the State to pay compensation of Rs.2 lakhs each to the heirs of 36 deceased persons and Rs.1.50 lakhs each to those blinded by the spurious liquor. However, the Supreme Court did not interfere with this order as the compensation had already been disbursed.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution case centered around a tragic incident where 36 persons died and 44 persons lost their eyesight after consuming spurious liquor purchased from a licensed liquor vend. Medical evidence confirmed that the cause of death and loss of vision was due to the consumption of liquor adulterated with methyl alcohol. Victims and their relatives stated they purchased the liquor from the respondents' vend, which was corroborated by the conduct of the respondents in disposing of remaining stock after the incident. The prosecution presented evidence showing the respondents were licensed vendors and that they had knowledge of the harmful effects of the liquor they sold. The trial court convicted the respondents for their involvement in the sale of spurious liquor, while the High Court initially acquitted them, citing lack of evidence. The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's acquittal, finding sufficient evidence to connect the respondents to the tragedy.

title: STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH versus RAJ KUMAR

neutral_facts: The accused, who was living with the victim and her children, was involved in an altercation with the victim on the night of the incident. The victim was heard crying and was seen being taken away by the accused towards another person's house. Later, the victim's body was found hanging from a tree. The accused did not report the victim's disappearance or inform the police, and no reasonable explanation was provided for the victim's death. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including the accused's failure to report the incident and the victim's last seen alive with the accused.

number_of_offences: Multiple offences/counts charged, but only the accused Raj Kumar was finally upheld for conviction under Section 302 IPC
motive: Frequent quarrels, assault, and greed for the fixed deposit of Rs.1,20,000/- due to be payable to the deceased
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted circumstantial evidence, including the testimony of PW-1, the deceased's son, and the autopsy report indicating that the death was due to hanging, which was post-mortem, along with the accused's failure to report the missing of the deceased.
witness_credibility: The court assessed PW-1's evidence as cogent, natural, and consistent with the prosecution case, rejecting the High Court's doubts about his credibility based on alleged improvements in his statement.
post_offence_conduct: The accused did not report the missing of the deceased nor inform the police, which the court considered a strong militating circumstance against him.

title: BHASKARRAO & ORS. versus STATE OF MAHARASHTRA

neutral_facts: The accused, a group of sixteen individuals, were alleged to have assaulted and killed the deceased during a dispute over money. The deceased's wife, who was the primary witness, claimed that the accused entered her home, dragged the deceased out, and assaulted him, eventually cutting off his right hand. The deceased's body was found in a field without his hand. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including witness statements and recovered weapons. However, the witnesses provided inconsistent accounts, and there were no independent witnesses to corroborate the prosecution's case. The medical evidence did not support the claim that the deceased's hand was amputated by the accused.

physical_harm: Death caused by amputation of the hand
number_of_offences: 16 accused charged; 15 finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt due to contradictions in witness statements, lack of independent witnesses, and inconsistencies in the evidence.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as having interest in the result, which affected their testimony, and noted that their statements were contradictory and inconsistent, thus undermining their credibility.
trial_duration: Trial judgment: 21.12.2013; High Court decision: 21.12.2013; Supreme Court decision: APRIL 26, 2018

defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. witness_credibility: The court assessed the injured witnesses PW-3 and PW-4 as credible, as their statements led to the lodging of the First Information Report and were corroborated by the post-mortem report.

legal_representation: Ravi Prakash Mehrotra, Ankit Agarwal, Ms. Deepti R. Mehrotra, Advs. for the Appellants; Ms. Jesal Wahi (for Ms. Hemantika Wahi), Adv. for the Respondent

legal_principle_applied: The right of private defence is to protect the person and the property. There were beatings from both sides, and the accused fled after the intervention of other villagers. The victim sustained fatal injuries from a single blow to the head, which was intentional. The accused were found to be the aggressors, and the incident escalated into a free fight. The prosecution's case was based on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence, which indicated the accused's intent to kill.

title: SURINDER SINGH versus STATE (UNION TERRITORY OF CHANDIGARH)
case_title: Surinder Singh v. State (Union Territory of Chandigarh)
aggravating_circumstances: Use of a service pistol, inebriated condition, pointing gun at victim
mitigating_circumstances: No motive or planning, clean record, passage of time, no injury caused

After consuming water, he pulled out his service pistol and aimed it at the victim, directing the victim's clerk and steno to leave the room. The accused moved around the table, pulled the lever of the pistol, and prepared to fire. The victim lunged at the accused, causing the bullet to hit the ceiling. The accused attempted to fire again but failed, and a bullet fell from the pistol. The incident was reported to the police, and the accused was arrested. Forensic evidence confirmed that the cartridge recovered from the victim's office was fired from the accused's service pistol. witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their testimonies corroborated each other and were supported by forensic evidence. The court found the defense's version of events to be 'a patch of lies and figment of imagination' and rejected it entirely.

The accused claimed an alternate version of events, but the trial court found it dubious. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts, medical reports, and forensic evidence to establish the accused's actions.

title: JAIKAM KHAN versus THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH
case_title: JAIKAM KHAN v. THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH
neutral_facts: The accused, who were four brothers, were involved in a dispute over the management of a brick-kiln. The prosecution alleged that they murdered six individuals at different locations within a house. The victims included the accused's father, mother, brother, sister-in-law, nephew, and niece. The prosecution relied on the testimonies of two witnesses, who were closely related to both the accused and the deceased. These witnesses described the events, including the locations where the victims were killed. The prosecution also presented evidence of weapons and bloodstained clothes, but the court questioned the credibility of these items due to lack of independent witnesses and inconsistencies in the evidence. The accused were arrested shortly after the incident, but the court found that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.

number_of_offences: Three counts were finally upheld against accused Nos. 1, 3 and 4
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation and planning as the accused had planned the murders and changed clothes to avoid detection
motive: Dispute over the management of the brick-kiln between the accused and deceased Mausam Khan, deceased Shaukeen Khan, and P.W.1
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to the unreliability of the main witnesses and lack of corroboration.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (P.W.1 and P.W.2) as neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable, requiring greater care and corroboration for conviction.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 23rd January, 2014; Trial judgment: 2nd January, 2016; High Court decision: 18th May, 2018; Supreme Court decision: 15th December, 2021

They also relied on the site-plans, recovery of weapons, and bloodstained clothes as evidence, and claimed that the accused had a motive related to a dispute over the management of the brick-kiln.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the eye-witnesses (P.W.1 and P.W.2) were closely related to the deceased and accused, and therefore their testimonies could not be considered wholly reliable. They also pointed out that the prosecution failed to examine independent witnesses, and that the recovery of weapons and bloodstained clothes lacked credibility. The defence also highlighted inconsistencies in the prosecution's case and the lack of corroboration.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the prosecution must prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, and that the testimony of interested and related witnesses must be scrutinized with due care and caution. sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, and the conviction and death sentence were deemed unsustainable in law.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who were four brothers, were involved in a dispute over the management of a brick-kiln. These witnesses described the events, including the locations where the victims were killed. However, the court found that the witnesses' testimonies were not reliable enough to support a conviction without additional corroboration. The prosecution also presented evidence of weapons and bloodstained clothes, but the court questioned the credibility of these items due to lack of independent witnesses and inconsistencies in the evidence. The accused were arrested shortly after the incident, but the court found that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.

title: KANCHAN SHARMA versus STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ANR.
case_title: Kanchan Sharma v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.306, s.3(2)(v) of the SC and ST Act
neutral_facts: The accused, a woman, was approached by the deceased, a man, who visited her house and consumed poison from a small bottle he carried in his pocket. The accused and her father had previously complained to the police about the deceased's behavior. The prosecution alleged that the accused abetted the deceased's suicide and committed casteist abuse. title: KALA SINGH @ GURNAM SINGH versus STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: KALA SINGH @ GURNAM SINGH v. STATE OF PUNJAB
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304 Part II r/w s.34; IPC s.201
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel; no pre-meditation; no intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302/34 and s.201 IPC
high_court_outcome: Modified conviction to s.304 Part-I/34 IPC

neutral_facts: The accused and the deceased had a sudden fight over a stolen pigeon. The co-accused, who had a rod, struck the deceased on the head with the rod, causing his death. physical_harm: Death caused
number_of_offences: Charged with 2 offences, 2 offences upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the scuffle had taken place on the spur of the moment and a sudden fight had taken place in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and there was no pre-meditation or intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses' credibility by noting that the evidence on record indicated the scuffle occurred spontaneously and that there was no intention to kill, supporting the conclusion that the conviction should be modified from Section 304 Part-I to Section 304 Part-II IPC.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: Not stated; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: 08.02.2019 and 01.03.2019; Supreme Court decision: September 21, 2021

investigation_status: Charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Sections 302/34 and 201 IPC; High Court: Modified conviction to Section 304 Part-I/34 IPC and maintained conviction under Section 201 IPC; Supreme Court: Modified conviction to Section 304 Part-II/34 IPC and maintained conviction under Section 201 IPC
prosecution_argument: The State of Punjab argued that the High Court's conviction of the appellant under Section 304 Part-I IPC was incorrect and that there were no grounds to interfere with the High Court's judgment. defence_argument: The appellant's counsel argued that there was no intention to kill the deceased, the scuffle was a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and it was not a pre-meditated act. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that if there was no intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, the conviction under Section 304 Part-I IPC should be modified to Section 304 Part-II IPC.

title: JASDEEP SINGH @ JASSU versus STATE OF PUNJAB

physical_harm: Death caused to the deceased
number_of_offences: Four offences/counts charged; three finally upheld

legal_representation: Counsel for the accused and the State in the Supreme Court: Shekhar Naphade, Siddharth Luthra, Vikram Chaudhri, Sr. Advs., Rajat Bali, Shivram, Gaurav Agrawal, Ms. Aishwarya Dash, Ms. Supriya Juneja, Ms. Shubhangi Jain, Ms. Sonali Sharma, Pankaj Singhal, Yash Giri, Nikhil Jain, Rishi Sehgal, Keshavam Chaudhari, Ms. Ria Khanna, Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Karanvir Gogia, Ms. Shivangi Singhal, Ms. Vamika Gupta, Advs.

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused A3 and A4 instigated A1 to shoot the deceased, and that the common intention under Section 34 IPC was established. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that Section 34 IPC creates a deeming fiction by attributing an offence committed by one to others acting in furtherance of a common intention. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that for conviction under Section 306 IPC, there must be evidence of instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid by the accused, and that the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused abetted the suicide.
precedent_relied_upon: M. Mohan vs. The State Represented By The Deputy Superintendent of Police (2011) 3 SCC 626 : [2011] 3 SCR 437; Mangat Ram vs. State of Haryana (2014) 12 SCC 595 : [2014] 4 SCR 988
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the conviction under Section 498A was upheld, but the appellants were acquitted of the charges under Section 306 due to lack of satisfactory evidence. The appellants had already served two years of imprisonment for the Section 498A conviction, so they were set free.
neutral_facts_raw: The deceased, a woman, married one of the accused approximately three years prior to the incident. The accused, who were the deceased's in-laws, were alleged to have subjected her to physical and mental harassment due to dowry demands. The deceased was found dead in a well, and the prosecution alleged that the accused had harassed her to the point of suicide. The prosecution relied on the testimony of the deceased's parents and uncle, as well as a neighbor, to establish the harassment. However, the evidence did not conclusively show that the accused had instigated or aided the deceased in committing suicide. The post-mortem report indicated the cause of death was drowning due to asphyxia, but there was no evidence to determine whether the death was accidental or suicidal. The prosecution failed to establish that the accused had abetted the deceased's suicide, despite the harassment allegations.

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that a verbal altercation between the parties resulted in a fight where the first informant was assaulted on the head and the deceased suffered severe assault leading to his death. defence_argument: The defence counsel suggested that the eyewitnesses' accounts were unreliable and that the accused could not be held guilty based on the prosecution's evidence. sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the deceased suffered severe injuries caused by dangerous weapons applied to his vital parts, which constitutes a case under Section 302 of the IPC. The court found that the appellants inflicted multiple blows on an unarmed and helpless person, which does not fall under Exception 4 to Section 300.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The aggravating factors weighed by the court included the use of dangerous weapons on the vital parts of the body, the infliction of multiple blows on an unarmed and helpless person, and the fact that the incident occurred in the heat of the moment and was sudden.
other_sentence_order: The appellants were ordered to surrender before the Trial Court within two weeks and to serve their sentence. Their bail bonds were cancelled.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused and the victim were strangers who engaged in a verbal altercation that escalated into a physical fight. witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as not credible, noting that the defense witnesses did not inspire confidence and the appellant's failure to inform the deceased's parents immediately after the incident smacked of guilt.

witness_credibility: The evidence of the wife was unimpeachable and could not be discarded on the basis that she was an interested witness. witness_credibility: The court assessed that the approver, once his pardon was forfeited, was relegated to the position of an accused and thus his evidence was not considered credible for the purposes of the trial of the co-accused. high_court_outcome: Convicted of the offence u/s. 302 IPC and awarded sentence of life imprisonment

She provided detailed information in the FIR, which was filed shortly after the incident. physical_harm: Fatal injuries by axe to temporal region, nose and face
number_of_offences: Number of offences/counts charged: 1, Number finally upheld: 1
key_evidence_accepted: The High Court wholly relied on the direct testimony of PW-1 and carefully examined her evidence threadbare. The High Court correctly found that she had a close relation with the accused who was her real brother-in-law and she was not expected to commit any mistake in identifying him; that she would certainly be interested in naming the culprit since she had lost her husband; and that she was a natural witness and her presence in her own household was also absolutely natural.
witness_credibility: PW-1 was thoroughly cross-examined and nothing could be brought out in her cross-examination which would bring her testimony into disrepute. She lodged the FIR barely within 4-41/2 hours of the accident. There is clear endorsement by the Magistrate that the FIR reached the Magistrate at 7.30 in the morning. Once this aspect of the timing is proved, the same must clinch the issue and then it cannot be imagined that PW-1 who was in the company of her relatives on her husband's side, would falsely implicate her own brother-in-law. The lady is illiterate. She could not have just created the theory that it was her brother-in-law who was the culprit, unless that was the truth. On this backdrop, when the FIR is read it completely corroborates her evidence.

The defense claimed that the deceased was not picked up from his house but from a Chowk and that injuries were noticed at the time of arrest. title: BALJINDER KAUR versus STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: Baljinder Kaur v. State of Punjab
high_court_outcome: Confirmed conviction of the appellant and Pritam Singh
neutral_facts: The accused, Baljinder Kaur, was the sister-in-law of the deceased, Sharanjit Kaur. The deceased married Pritam Singh in January 1997. After two months of marriage, the deceased informed her father and the mediator about the husband and his family members demanding dowry and harassing her. The accused demanded a gold bangle as dowry two months after the marriage. The deceased returned to her father's house due to the dowry demand, but was sent back to her husband's house after one month. She returned to her father's house again with the same demand. Two days before her death, the accused took her back to the matrimonial house. The deceased was found in critical condition and died of poisoning on the way to the hospital. The police registered an FIR under Section 304B IPC, and the accused were charged with dowry death. The prosecution argued that the accused subjected the deceased to cruelty and harassment for dowry demands soon before her death.
physical_harm: Poisoning leading to death
number_of_offences: Four offences charged, two upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of the father of the deceased (PW-4) regarding the alleged 'dying declaration' and the demand of gold karra by the appellant, but found that the investigation lacked credibility and did not focus on the contents of the complaint.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of PW-4 (father of the deceased) and PW-5 (Darshan Singh) as providing the main evidence, but noted that their testimony did not establish a proximate live link between the dowry demand and the death of the deceased.
bail_history: The appellant is on bail. The bail bond shall stand discharged.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 25.08.1997; Trial judgment: 11.08.2010; High Court decision: 11.08.2010; Supreme Court decision: 19.11.2014

They also emphasized that the investigation was flawed and the evidence was insufficient.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the proximity test, emphasizing that for a conviction under Section 304B IPC, there must be a proximate and live link between the cruelty or harassment related to dowry demand and the death of the victim, with the cruelty occurring 'soon before death'.

title: M.B. SURESH versus STATE OF KARNATAKA

witness_credibility: The court noted that the prosecution's case was that the deceased died of shock, but there was no evidence to show that the shock was caused by the injuries inflicted by the appellant.
